The Red Sox begin the postseason on Tuesday and have scored just 5 runs over the last 5 games. In other words, now would be a great time for the team's best offensive contributor to return to a lineup that desperately needs a spark. But unless a miracle happens over the weekend, things aren't looking good. Willson Contreras took batting practice on Tuesday, only for his hand injury to worsen in the subsequent days. He's still struggling to grip a bat and admitted to tearing up out of frustration. "I'm doing everything that I can to come back and play with the boys and be there with the boys," he said. "But sometimes you have to listen to your body." (Tim Healey, Boston Globe)
At least Ceddanne Rafaela has returned. He should be able to give a little lift for the lineup, though he does present a conundrum for Chad Tracy, as the Sox now have too many outfielders and DHs to fit into the lineup at once. With Roman Anthony, Rafalea, and Wilyer Abreu essentially locked into starting spots, Tracy has to decide whether to prioritize Duran's glove and legs over the platoon DH production of Mickey Gasper and Jahmai Jones. (Sean McAdam, MassLive)
And all of this is occuring against the backdrop of this weekend's storm. And if you think we're done dealing with that now that MLB has moved Sunday's game to today, we're not. There is still a possibility that one or more of this weekend's games is moved to Tropicana Field in St. Pete. (Conor Ryan, Boston.com)
With the depressing news about Contreras, the team could probably use a pep talk. If so, Pedro Martinez — as someone who still believed in this team in the darkness of May — is available. "I just feel good about approaching the Yankees this time around. And [the Red Sox] are young, yes. We don't have the highest expectations about them, but man, for some reason, I just feel so positive," said the right arm of God. "I just feel so excited that this young group of guys that we have out there are able to do something special. I don't see anything wrong with these kids, and I don't see why they shouldn't give everybody knuckles. Not just the Yankees, but everybody." (Ian Browne, MLB.com)
If the Sox are going to give everybody knuckles, then Ranger Suarez is probably going to be a part of it. The offseason signing has an outstanding postseason resume, and his final 2026 stats are more or less in line with the numbers he'd been putting up in Philadelphia, even if he sounds slightly disappointed in his performance. "Obviously I think I could have done better," he said of his season. "But I was happy I was able to finish the season strong." (Peter Abraham, Boston Globe)

Field Level Media

25 Sep 2026, 12:10 GMT+10

(Photo credit: William Purnell)
Miguel Vargas had two hits and two RBIs, Kyle Teel homered and David Sandlin delivered six strong innings as the visiting Chicago White Sox routed the Kansas City Royals 9-1 on Thursday to clinch an American League playoff berth.
Chicago is back in the postseason for the first time since 2021 after enduring three straight 100-loss seasons.
Fueled by an early barrage against Royals right-hander Randy Dobnak, the White Sox remained a game behind the AL Central-leading Cleveland Guardians. Chicago holds the head-to-head tiebreaker over Cleveland. Whichever one of those two teams fails to win the division will wind up as the third AL wild-card team.
Sandlin (3-2) yielded one run and five hits. Dobnak (3-5) allowed six runs (four earned) and six hits in 1 1/3 innings.
Guardians 1, Red Sox 0
Angel Martinez's second-inning home run was all visiting Cleveland needed for a win over Boston to clinch its third consecutive playoff berth.
Joey Cantillo (11-9) dominated for five shutout innings as the Guardians' bulk reliever, yielding one hit. Hunter Gaddis, Erik Sabrowski and Cade Smith allowed a combined one hit over the final three innings to help Cleveland win its seventh game in the last eight.
The playoff-bound Red Sox fell for the fourth time in five games despite getting five innings of one-run ball from Ranger Suarez (8-5).
Cubs 2, Marlins 1
Nico Hoerner ripped a go-ahead RBI single in the sixth and Matthew Boyd tossed seven strong innings, helping host Chicago clinch a playoff berth with a victory over Miami.
Chicago's Pete Crow-Armstrong walked to lead off the first inning and promptly stole second base to become the seventh player in major league history to record at least 40 homers and 40 stolen bases in a single season.
Seiya Suzuki belted a solo homer in the fifth inning to highlight his two-hit performance for the Cubs, who salvaged the finale of their three-game series with Miami. Chicago sits in the second NL wild-card spot, one game behind San Diego.
Padres 4, Dodgers 2
Dustin Harris drove in the go-ahead run in the sixth inning as visiting San Diego beat Los Angeles to clinch a playoff spot for a franchise-record third consecutive season.
Yuki Matsui (4-1) earned the win with a scoreless inning, and Mason Miller gave up a run with two outs in the ninth before securing his 38th save. Ethan Salas and Fernando Tatis Jr. each had two hits and an RBI for the Padres.
Tyler Glasnow (5-2) fanned a season-high 11 but allowed three runs in 6 1/3 innings for the Dodgers, who secured a first-round playoff bye thanks to the Atlanta Braves' loss on Thursday. Shohei Ohtani went 2-for-5 with an RBI double.
Brewers 5, Phillies 1
Jake Bauers' RBI single in the eighth inning plated the go-ahead run for Milwaukee, which reached the 100-win mark for the first time in franchise history with a win at Philadelphia. When the Dodgers fell to the Padres later, the Brewers clinched the top record in the major leagues.
Bauers, who went 2-for-5, singled up the middle, allowing Jackson Chourio to score from second, giving the Brewers (100-59) a 2-1 lead and starting a three-run frame.
Philadelphia remains in an NL wild-card spot, but the Phillies could not drop their magic number to clinch from two. Phillies starter Andrew Painter threw six innings of one-run ball, fanning eight. Bryce Harper went 2-for-4 with an RBI.
Diamondbacks 12, Rockies 8
Gabriel Moreno and Nolan Arenado homered in a six-run first inning and surging Arizona beat Colorado in Denver to continue its drive for a wild-card berth.
James McCann also went deep for Arizona, which moved within two games of Philadelphia for the third and final NL playoff berth. Arizona finishes the regular season in San Diego while the Phillies host Tampa Bay this weekend.
Cole Carrigg homered among his four hits, Kyle Karros and Zac Veen also went deep and had two hits for Colorado, which finished with 17 hits.
Rangers 3, Mets 1
Kumar Rocker pitched five solid innings for Texas, which salvaged the finale of a three-game series against New York in Arlington, Texas.
Josh Jung (3-for-3) hit a two-run homer in the first and Corey Seager went deep in the sixth for the Rangers, who remain tied with Houston for first place in the American League West. Rocker (6-11) allowed one run on three hits. Jordan Montgomery recorded his first save of the season.
Mets starter Zac Thornton (5-6) yielded two runs on four hits over five innings. Brett Baty extended his on-base streak to 17 games.
Astros 7, Athletics 5
Rookie Lucas Spence hit his first three career homers and drove in five runs as Houston smacked five homers while defeating the Athletics in West Sacramento, Calif.
Isaac Paredes and Christian Walker added solo blasts for the Astros who remained tied for first in the AL West with the Rangers. Houston holds the tiebreaker, having gone 9-4 vs. Texas this year.
Houston reliever Miguel Ullola (2-0) fired three scoreless innings and Brayan Abreu worked 1 1/3 shutout innings for his ninth save. Zack Gelof hit two homers and Jeff McNeil drilled a three-run shot for the Athletics, who lost for the seventh time in nine games.
Yankees 6, Rays 4
Rookie George Lombard Jr. hit a tiebreaking two-run homer with two outs in the eighth inning as New York overcame a four-run deficit and earned a victory over visiting Tampa Bay.
New York ace Cam Schlittler allowed two runs (one earned) in three innings in a playoff tuneup, ending the season with a 1.95 ERA. Bradley Hanner (1-0) threw two scoreless innings for his first career victory.
Junior Caminero had a pair of RBI singles for the Rays. Ian Seymour allowed one hit in five scoreless innings. Steven Matz (5-6) served up Lombard's decisive homer.
Pirates 2, Cardinals 1
Spencer Horwitz's sacrifice fly in the eighth drove in the go-ahead run, and Paul Skenes concluded his season with a quality start as Pittsburgh wrapped up its home schedule with a victory over St. Louis.
Skenes tossed 6 1/3 innings, struck out eight, walked two and allowed one run on three hits. His final pitch completed a strikeout of Leo Bernal, giving him 200-plus for the second straight season. Luke Weaver (4-1) escaped an inherited eighth-inning jam before Mason Montgomery recorded his 17th save.
Alec Burleson homered for the Cardinals. St. Louis (77-82) is guaranteed to finish with back-to-back losing seasons for the first time since 1994-95.
Reds 7, Braves 6
A two-run homer by Hector Rodriguez, one of three long balls by Cincinnati, helped the visiting Reds beat Atlanta in the rubber game of a three-game series.
Rodriguez clubbed a 423-foot homer to right field against AJ Smith-Shawver (0-3) in the sixth inning to give the Reds the lead for good. Elly De La Cruz added his 30th homer and Carlos Jorge hit his first career homer. Cincinnati reliever Connor Phillips (2-0) pitched 1 1/3 scoreless innings.
Atlanta right-hander Tyler Mahle threw five innings and gave up five runs on six hits in his worst outing since being acquired from San Francisco at the trade deadline.
Angels 6, Mariners 4
Christian Moore doubled, singled and drove in three runs as Los Angeles won at Seattle.
Josh Lowe also had a single and a double and scored three times for the Angels. Los Angeles starter Grayson Rodriguez (5-8) gave up four runs on five hits over five innings. Ryan Watson pitched the ninth for his fourth save.
Julio Rodriguez homered for the Mariners, whose postseason hopes were dashed when the Rangers defeated the Mets earlier in the day. Bryan Woo (12-10) allowed five runs, four earned, on seven hits in 5 1/3 innings.

The Red Sox made their biggest investment of the offseason in January when they signed free agent lefthander Ranger Suarez for five years and $130 million.
Eight months later, it’s fair to say Suarez did what was expected.
He was 8-5 with a 3.22 earned run average over 28 starts and 148 innings. Suarez was an All-Star, and the Sox were 17-11 in the games he started. Outside of missing three starts with a groin strain and a sore lower back, Suarez was a reliable rotation pillar.
He allowed one earned run or none in 16 starts. That’s right in line with how he pitched for the Phillies in 2024 and ’25.
Suarez allowed one run on three hits over five innings in a 1-0 loss against the Guardians on Thursday night. The one run came on a 319-foot Pesky Pole home run by Angel Martinez in the second inning.
Otherwise, Suarez stayed in control despite throwing 39 pitches over the first two innings.
“When you look at the body of work, especially coupled with the other guys in the rotation, he was fantastic,” manager Chad Tracy said. “He had a great year.”
Suarez wasn’t quite so complimentary of himself.
“In general, good,” he said via a translator. “Obviously I think I could have done better. But I was happy I was able to finish the season strong.”
Now comes the true test.
Suarez was 4-1 with a 1.48 ERA in 11 postseason games for the Phillies, eight of them as a starter. Philadelphia won eight of those games.
That includes Game 3 of the Division Series against the Dodgers last season when Suarez pitched five innings out of the bullpen and held the mighty Dodgers to one run at Dodger Stadium. That’s what he’s capable of in a big game.
Suarez is likely to start Game 3 in the Wild Card Series next week, which means he could have a huge say in whether this memorable season will continue.
“Being able to finish this month strong, I think, is going to be the key for the playoffs,” Suarez said.
Suarez was referring to the 1.09 ERA and 0.93 WHIP he posted over his final four starts.
His results against the Yankees this season were less encouraging. Suarez faced them three times and allowed 11 earned runs over 16 innings.
But he did have a strong start at Yankee Stadium on June 7, allowing one run over 6 innings against Cam Schlittler. It was 1-1 when Suarez left the game; then the bullpen allowed five runs.
Tracy has not revealed his rotation for the series. But if he stays in order, it would be Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Suarez.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone has held back that information, too.
Schlittler, who is a heavy favorite to win the Cy Young Award, would make sense to start Game 1. He dominated the Sox in four starts this season, allowing two earned runs over 24 innings and striking out 27.
A Tolle-Schlittler matchup would be must-viewing for even a casual baseball fan.
But there is speculation that the Yankees would save Schlittler for Game 2 and give Game 1 to lefthander Max Fried, who also has pitched well against the Sox this season.
That might be overthinking it, but it’s an option.
Based on the last few games, the Red Sox will need their pitchers to be close to perfect. Tracy has used the last 10 days to give his regulars rest while giving extra time off to players who have been dealing with injuries.
The Sox have scored only five runs over their last five games and hit .222. Willson Contreras, who was thought to be progressing well from a bruised right hand, said after the game he was concerned about being ready for the Yankees series.
“I’m doing everything that I can to come back and play with the boys and be with them,” Suarez said. “But sometimes you have to listen to your body.”
If Contreras can’t play, or is compromised, that would put even more pressure on the pitchers.
“This team can pitch,” Suarez said. “We’ll be ready for next week.”

Guardians eke out 1-0 win over Red Sox, clinch playoff berth
(Photo credit: Paul Rutherford)
Angel Martinez's second-inning home run was all the visiting Guardians needed for a 1-0 win over the Boston Red Sox on Thursday night, allowing Cleveland to clinch its third consecutive American League playoff berth.
While Martinez provided the only offense, Joey Cantillo (11-9) dominated for five shutout innings behind opener Daniel Espino. Cantillo allowed just one hit and two walks and striking out four. He has not allowed a run across his last three outings (15 innings) as a bulk reliever.
The Guardians (83-76) totaled four hits but allowed only two to the Red Sox (85-74) en route to winning the decisive game of the three-game series. Boston earned a 1-0 victory on Wednesday.
Cleveland logged its seventh win in eight games to remain one game ahead of the Chicago White Sox (82-77) atop the AL Central. Both teams have three regular-season games remaining.
The playoff-bound Red Sox fell for the fourth time in five games despite getting five innings of one-run ball from Ranger Suarez (8-5). He struck out five and allowed three hits and one walk.
Espino bookended his 1-2-3 first inning with strikeouts.
The lone run came in the second, as Martinez broke up Suarez's four-up, four-down start with a 319-foot solo homer inside Pesky's Pole in right field.
Suarez escaped a two-on jam in the third with back-to-back outs and retired the final eight Guardians he faced.
Both bullpens were very strong. Hunter Gaddis allowed the sole hit in relief of Cantillo, a Jarren Duran single in the seventh, but they came after a leadoff walk in the frame was erased in a 6-4-3 double play.
Cleveland's Erik Sabrowski struck out two in the eighth, and Cade Smith fanned the side in a 1-2-3 ninth for his 41st save of the season.
Boston's Patrick Sandoval, Erik Miller and Raymond Burgos allowed just one combined hit across four shutout innings after Suarez departed. Burgos pitched hitless ball over the final two frames.
--Field Level Media

In these waning days of the regular season, the Red Sox are trying something new: Patrick Sandoval, reliever.
Sandoval tossed a scoreless sixth inning in a 1-0 loss to the Guardians on Thursday, his first appearance out of the bullpen since 2021.
It was a successfully uneventful frame at Fenway Park: After José Ramírez grounded a single through the left side of the infield and stole second, Sandoval retired Chase DeLauter (strikeout looking), Jo Adell (ground out), and Angel Martínez (ground out). His velocity was down a tad in the small sample size of 12 pitches (10 strikes), but he was pitching just three days after his most recent start.
Ahead of the playoffs opening Tuesday, the Sandoval twist is of particular note because of his recent struggles as a starter and the Red Sox’ recent struggles looking for a reliable lefthanded reliever.
As a member of the rotation, Sandoval had a 5.15 ERA in 13 outings this year. That included a 7.32 mark in four starts this month. He has appeared unlikely to fit into the postseason plans in that role.
Also of late, Erik Miller, the team’s top lefty reliever, has had a bad time, entering the day with a 8.53 ERA in seven appearances this month. Of the 36 hitters he had faced, 17 had reached base: six hits, a whopping nine walks, and two batters hit by pitches.
Immediately after Sandoval departed, though, Miller entered — and maybe figured it out. He turned in a perfect seventh on just eight pitches, getting a strikeout of David Fry, a routine fly out from Travis Bazzana, and a 108-miles-per-hour line out from Patrick Bailey.
The loss dropped the Red Sox to 85-74 and — with three games to go — ensured that they will not match their 89 wins from last year.
They totaled two hits. Nick Sogard and Jarren Duran each had a single. It was the fourth game this month in which the Sox recorded four hits or fewer.
Lefthander Ranger Suarez finished a strong September — and strong regular season — with five innings of one-run ball. He held the Guardians to three hits and a walk and struck out five.
Cleveland’s lone run against him came on Martínez’s home run, tucked inside the Pesky Pole, an estimated 319 feet down the right-field line. It came off his bat at only 94 m.p.h. The batted ball had an expected batting average of .160.
At the end of the first season of a five-year, $130 million contract, Suarez owns a 3.22 ERA, third best in the Red Sox’ rotation behind righthander Sonny Gray (2.72) and lefthander Payton Tolle (3.03).
Suarez suffered from a midseason dip — a groin injury followed by mediocrity — but rebounded late, posting a 1.09 ERA over his final four starts.
The Sox mustered minimal offense against opener Daniel Espino (perfect first inning with two strikeouts) and lefthander Joey Cantillo (one hit and no runs in five innings).
For Cantillo, who entered the night with the most walks in the American League (79) but issued just two free passes against the Red Sox, it was his third consecutive scoreless appearance. In all three, he entered behind an opener.

With the coming nor’easter hitting town this weekend, the Red Sox and Guardians have played with an October chill in the air this week.
The Red Sox halted their three-game slide with a 1-0 win on Wednesday. Andrew Monasterio’s RBI single in the bottom of the sixth held as the eventual winner after Sonny Gray dealt six shutout innings.
That came after the Guardians won Tuesday’s contest, 3-2, setting up Thursday’s game as the series rubber match.
Given his postgame comments, the Red Sox hope to have avoided a scare regarding center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela, who left his first game back from the injured list with right hamstring tightness. A quad injury sent him to the IL on Sept. 3.
“Not even close,” Rafaela said of the severity comparison of the two injuries. “I think it was just a cramp.”
After the game, Tracy said Rafaela would have an MRI exam on Thursday.
Ranger Suarez will start for the Red Sox on Thursday. He’s 1-1 with a 4.00 ERA in four career appearances, including three starts, against Cleveland. On May 31, he struck out 10 and allowed four runs across five frames against Cleveland in Boston’s 9-4 win.
“He’s a very good competitor, a good pitcher that even when he gets traffic, you trust that he’s going to find his way through it,” Tracy said of Suarez, whose ERA in three September starts is 0.92.
Daniel Espino will open for Cleveland before giving way to Joey Cantillo.

By KEN POWTAK
Updated 10:25 PM EDT, September 23, 2026
BOSTON (AP) — Sonny Gray pitched six innings to tie Philadelphia’s Cristopher Sánchez for the major league lead with his 18th victory, Andruw Monasterio drove in the only run with a sixth-inning single, and the Boston Red Sox edged Cleveland 1-0 on Wednesday night to snap the Guardians’ six-game winning streak.
It was just the fifth win in 13 games for the Red Sox, who clinched a playoff spot on Sunday.
The 36-year-old Gray (18-5) is in line to become the fourth Red Sox pitcher since 2000 to lead the AL in victories, joining Rick Porcello (2016), Josh Beckett (’07) and Curt Schilling (’04).
Gray allowed four singles, struck out three, walked one and lowered his ERA to 2.72.
Aroldis Chapman struck out the side in the ninth for his 35th save of the season.
Cleveland starter Foster Griffin (15-6) gave up a run on 10 hits with seven strikeouts.
The Guardians remained one game ahead of the Chicago White Sox atop the AL Central, after Chicago lost 5-4 to Kansas City on Wednesday night. The Guardians needed a win Wednesday combined with a loss by either Texas or Houston to clinch a postseason berth.
The victory came with a price for the Red Sox when center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela left with right hamstring tightness after running out a single the same day he was activated from the injured list. He had been sidelined with a right a quad strain since Sept. 3 and made a diving headlong grab on Steven Kwan, the game’s first batter.
Jarren Duran singled leading off the sixth, advanced on a groundout and barely beat left fielder Kwan’s throw with a headfirst slide on Monasterio’s hit.
Up next
Red Sox LHP Ranger Suarez (8-4, 3.27 ERA) is slated to start the series finale Thursday. The Guardians had not named a starter.

The 30-year-old outfielder stole his 20th base of the season on Wednesday night, joining an exclusive club in team history.
BOSTON -- The Boston Red Sox beat the Cleveland Guardians 1-0 on Wednesday night to improve to 85-73 and set up a rubber match on Thursday night. It was supposed to be a night off for struggling outfielder Jarren Duran; however, after center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela exited the game in the third inning with a right hamstring injury, the 30-year-old Duran was thrust into action, joining an exclusive list in the franchise's 125-year history in the process.
Duran's first at-bat in the third inning ended in disappointment as he struck out with the bases loaded to end the scoring chance for Boston. However, the 30-year-old turned in a strong performance in relief of the injured Rafaela, leading off the bottom of the sixth inning with a single, later coming around to score the game's lone run on a single off the bat of second baseman Andruw Monasterio.
Duran again reached base leading off the eighth inning with a sharply hit line drive to right field. With Boston leading 1-0, the speedster did everything he could to get the team in a position to add on. With third baseman Caleb Durbin at the plate, Duran took off for second base, diving in safely for his 20th stolen base of the year, securing the second 20-home-run, 20-steal season of his career.
Duran became just the third player in Red Sox history to post multiple 20/20 seasons, joining 2018 Most Valuable Player Mookie Betts, who did so three times during his six-year tenure in Boston, and Jackie Jensen, who accomplished the feat twice.
Reaching 20 home runs and 20 steals is an impressive accomplishment for Duran in an otherwise unimpressive season. The 30-year-old has been one of baseball's most disappointing players in 2026, hitting just .207/.265/.364/.629 in 147 games. The 30-year-old ranks in the bottom five among 133 qualified hitters in batting average (129th), on-base percentage (133rd), and OPS (131st).
Despite those struggles, Duran has still found a way to provide some value to the team in both the power and speed departments.
In other Red Sox news
Manager Chad Tracy told reporters, including Tim Healey of the Boston Globe, that Rafaela will undergo an MRI on his right hamstring. Rafaela described the injury as "cramping" that he felt on a swing, rather than when he ran to first base on his second-inning single.
As reported by MassLive.com's Chris Cotillo, 2025 Cy Young Award runner-up Garrett Crochet is scheduled to throw another live bullpen session this weekend as he tries to return from left shoulder inflammation and join the Red Sox in a bullpen role for the postseason. Crochet will not make a regular-season appearance before potentially joining the active roster for the Wild Card round.
With a nor'easter expected to hit New England beginning Friday night, Major League Baseball has moved the Red Sox regular-season finale to Friday afternoon as part of a day-night doubleheader, starting at 1:05 p.m. ET. The league also moved up the start time for Friday's regularly scheduled game from 7:10 p.m. ET to 6:05 p.m. ET. As of now, no changes have been made to Saturday's game.
Up next for the Sox
The Red Sox will look to win the series from the Guardians in Thursday night's rubber match at Fenway Park. Ranger Suarez (8-4, 3.27 ERA) will make his final regular-season start for Boston, while Cleveland has not yet named its starter. First pitch is set for 6:45 p.m. ET.

The Yankees had to make do without Aaron Judge for all of June, July and August due to a stress fracture in his right first rib. With the days on the calendar dwindling and the AL East title still in play — which is no longer the case after the Rays clinched on Tuesday night — Judge bypassed a rehab assignment, but once he returned, he played in just seven games before landing back on the injured list due to a right calf strain. Both the slugger and the team took great pains to avoid discussing the injury’s specificity and timeline for recovery until Tuesday, when manager Aaron Boone revealed that Judge has a “moderate grade” strain, received a platelet-poor plasma injection, and isn’t expected to be available for the team’s Wild Card Series rematch against the Red Sox.
While deadline acquisition Heliot Ramos has heated up after a very slow start to his pinstriped career, the Yankees’ right field situation is one of the more glaring potential trouble spots among American League contenders. As the playoffs approach, teams no longer have a chance to upgrade from outside their organizations and instead must make do with the talent on hand. What follows here is a look at the most vulnerable teams at each position — something of a companion to my annual pre-deadline Replacement Level Killers series, with a focus on the teams that still have a chance to make the playoffs. For the AL, that means the Rays, Yankees, and Red Sox — all of whom have clinched spots — plus the Guardians, White Sox, Rangers, and Astros, who are battling for the other two division titles and the third Wild Card spot. I’ve taken the Blue Jays out of consideration, as their Playoff Odds now start with a zero in front of the decimal. While full-season performances play a significant part here, I’m more concerned with who’s worst now, with injuries and adjustments in mind. Each position has a headliner (or two, if it’s a job share), but at several positions, I’ve noted other teams with concerns. A companion National League piece will follow.
Catcher: Kyle Teel and Jake Rogers, White Sox
A Top 100 prospect in both 2024 and ’25, Kyle Teel did a very solid job as a rookie last season, hitting for a 125 wRC+ with 1.9 WAR in just 78 games, but he missed the first two months of this season due to a Grade 2 right hamstring strain and then an LCL sprain in his right knee. His replacements, mainly Edgar Quero (a three-time Top 100 prospect) and Drew Romo, struggled so mightily that they headed the catchers’ section on my Replacement Level Killers list, with Quero optioned to Triple-A Charlotte once Teel returned. While Teel’s defense has been an upgrade, he’s hit just .178/.302/.318 (81 wRC+) with an astronomical 37.3% strikeout rate, up from last year’s 25.9%, and his average exit velocity is just 84.5 mph, down from last year’s 88.3 mph. He recently missed time with a left ankle sprain as well.
Romo was optioned to Charlotte in early September during a shuffle that included both Teel’s return and the arrival of the 31-year-old Jake Rogers via the waiver wire. Rogers, who began the year with the Tigers, was traded to the Orioles in late July, then flipped to the Red Sox in the Adley Rutschman trade on August 3 before being sent on his merry way again within a fortnight. He’s now playing for his fourth team this season and has hit just .161/.276/.287 (62 wRC+). All told, White Sox catchers have combined for a 54 wRC+ and -0.4 WAR, both of which rank 29th in the majors; for as much long-term potential as the 24-year-old Teel and 23-year-old Quero (who has played sparingly since being recalled) may have, they’re less than ideal right now.
It’s worth noting that Rutschman, who was on the injured list due to left wrist inflammation when he was sent to Boston as part of a seven-player blockbuster, has struggled to the point that he’s a concern as well. The 28-year-old switch-hitter was batting a solid .251/.331/.433 (116 wRC+) before being sidelined for three weeks — his third IL stint this season, with shorter ones for left ankle inflammation and a concussion while with Baltimore — but he’s hit just .214/.270/.398 (82 wRC+) in 111 plate appearances since being activated. His strikeout rate has spiked from 14.1% to 21.6%, and his average exit velo has fallen by about two ticks. Backup Connor Wong has hit a similarly light .234/.310/.346 (84 wRC+), albeit with dreadful defense (-10 FRV, -8 DRS, -6.6 FRM). The good news is that Rutschman went 3-for-4 with a pair of doubles on Tuesday night against the Guardians; the bad news is that the Red Sox have other injury concerns in their lineup as well.
First Base: Nathaniel Lowe and David Fry, Guardians
Guardians first basemen made my Killers list due to the light production of their platoon of Kyle Manzardo and Rhys Hoskins. At the deadline, they dealt for Nathaniel Lowe and optioned Manzardo to Triple-A Columbus. A couple of week later, they placed Hoskins on the IL due to lower back inflammation and turned to David Fry, a utilityman who can catch. Alas, after getting a 94 wRC+ from their first basemen prior to the deadline, they’ve managed just a 90 wRC+ since. The lefty-swinging Lowe, who hit a robust .266/.341/.480 (123 wRC+) for the Reds, has dipped to .228/.279/.390 (83 wRC+) while hitting a ton of popups. The righty-swinging Fry has done well in his limited duty at first base, but has hit just .192/.312/.349 (90 wRC+) in 202 plate appearances overall.
Hoskins began a swing progression nearly two weeks ago, but with Columbus’ season having ended, a rehab assignment isn’t an option, which doesn’t bode well for an uptick from his .179/.306/.376 (95 wRC+) line. Manzardo (.215/.306/.378, 95 wRC+) didn’t hit the ball as hard at Columbus as he had either in his previous stops there or in Cleveland, and there hasn’t been any buzz about bringing him back in September or October.
Meanwhile in Boston, Willson Contreras has been the team’s top hitter, batting a potent .276/.387/.518 (152 wRC+) with 27 homers, but he’s been limited to four games this month between a left hamstring strain and a hit-by-pitch induced bruised knuckle on his right hand. Fortunately, he avoided a fracture, and returned to swinging a bat on September 20; the Red Sox hope to get him into the lineup before the end of the regular season, but the situation bears monitoring. Mickey Gasper and Nick Sogard have shared duties during his absence. Both have provided above-average production overall; Gasper had been in a 4-for-32 slump before hitting a pinch-homer — his 10th long ball in 218 plate appearances — against the Guardians on Tuesday night.
Second Base: Jose Altuve, Astros
Jose Altuve may wind up in Cooperstown some day, but Father Time has caught up to the diminutive 36-year-old. He’s batting just .250/.308/.402, which has taken a bite out of both the Astros’ offense and his chances at reaching 3,000 hits; his 99 wRC+ is his lowest full-season mark since 2013, while his .327 xSLG is a 57-point drop from last season and a Statcast-era low. What’s more, his defense has reached its nadir, with both his -10 FRV and -16 DRS rating not only as career worsts but also major league worsts at his position. With Yordan Alvarez entrenched at designated hitter and too valuable to risk in left field — he hasn’t used his glove in a postseason game since 2023 — there’s no place to hide Altuve, but also little likelihood he’ll be benched in favor of backup Nick Allen (.271/.318/.371, 95 wRC+).
On the injury front, keep an eye on the return of the Yankees’ Jazz Chisholm Jr., who was activated between games of Tuesday’s doubleheader against the Rays after missing 12 games due to a sprained right thumb. While his offense has dipped from a 125 wRC+ last year to 100 (.233/.313/.403) this year, Chisholm’s 3.4 WAR ranks third among the team’s position players behind Ben Rice and Cody Bellinger, and his total of 19 home runs ranks second. Backups Anthony Volpe (.244/.321/.335, 88 wRC+) and José Caballero (.236/.293/.373, 86 wRC+) are substantial steps down, but if Chisholm has any lingering issues, one of them may be needed to fill in.
Third Base: Ryan McMahon and Amed Rosario, Yankees
Yankees third basemen have combined for -0.1 WAR, the majors’ third-lowest mark. Lefty-swinging Ryan McMahon bears the bulk of the responsibility for that, hitting just .206/.274/.341 (73 wRC+) while playing solid defense. Righty-swinging Amed Rosario has produced a 100 wRC+ while playing third but has hit just .233/.275/.406 (87 wRC+) overall, and he’s been lousy at the hot corner, with -6 DRS and -6 FRV in just 309.1 innings. The righty-swinging Caballero is at least a better defender than Rosario and about on par offensively, and he’s one of the league’s top base thieves, with 34 steals in 45 attempts. He has also out-produced Rosario against lefties, with an 81 wRC+ to Rosario’s 63 — which could be a factor given that the Red Sox can call upon lefties Ranger Suarez and Payton Tolle to start during the Wild Card Series.
Shortstop: Taylor Walls, Rays
For the third year in a row, the defensive metrics have been very split with regards to Taylor Walls. His 21 DRS leads all shortstops (nobody else has more than 10 DRS), but his -2 FRV ranks 23rd out of 30 with at least 500 innings at the position. Between the latter mark and his dismal .222/.308/.294 (73 wRC+) line, he’s produced just 0.7 WAR. That said, neither Jorge Mateo (.205/.250/.318, 55 wRC+) nor Ben Williamson (.244/.304/.327, 79 wRC+), his occasional fill-ins, hits well enough to merit surpassing Wells on the depth chart.
Left Field: Taylor Trammell and LaMonte Wade Jr., Astros
The Astros’ current 1.3 WAR from their left fielders ranks 17th in the majors, ahead of both the Guardians (1.2) and Red Sox (0.8). But between Steven Kwan’s second-half heater and Roman Anthony’s return from a torn tendon in his right ring finger, both of those teams are now in a better spot than Houston. Taylor Trammell made several Top 100 lists as a prospect — he was as high as no. 12 as a 60-FV on our 2019 list — but he’s now 29 and has netted 0.1 WAR in 273 major league games for four different teams. This year he’s hit .200/.292/.355 (84 wRC+) in a career-high 95 games spread across the three outfield positions, with a 95 wRC+ in 237 plate appearances against righties and a 19 wRC+ (ouch) in 41 plate appearances against lefties.
LaMonte Wade Jr., a reliable contributor for the Giants from 2021–24, bottomed out to a 53 wRC+ last year in a season split between San Francisco and Anaheim. He spent the first few months of this season in the White Sox organization but was released on June 1 so he could sign with the Astros, for whom he’s hit .208/.308/.352 (90 wRC+). He’s been protected from facing many lefties and has seen his playing time dry up otherwise, as he’s been in a slump since mid-August. Meanwhile, righty-swinging Nelson Velázquez hasn’t made a very strong case for himself by hitting .192/.255/.414 (81 wRC+) with a 33.6% strikeout rate in 110 plate appearances split between the Cardinals and Astros. With options like these, you can see why playing Alvarez in left and DHing Altuve starts to make some sense.
Center Field: Daulton Varsho, Astros
The first-half struggles of Jake Meyers, Brice Matthews and Trammell landed the Astros on the Killers center field list, so they quite reasonably dealt for Daulton Varsho on August 3. The 30-year-old flychaser was hitting .243/.307/.375 (91 wRC+), and while his once-elite defense has regressed towards average, a performance like that is still good enough to carry the position. He looked like a decent upgrade for Houston, but while his defense has remained solid enough, he’s hit an anemic .172/.224/.311 (48 wRC+), with his strikeout and walk rates both moving in the wrong direction.
A closer look shows that Varsho has actually been hitting the ball slightly harder since the trade, but all season, he’s been producing popups and cans of corn galore because he’s getting under so many pitches. The real fall-off is relative to last year; his pulled air rate has fallen from 29.5% to 18.5%, while his xSLG has dropped from .464 to .354. As with Altuve and the left field situation, the Astros don’t have great alternatives. Matthews, a 24-year-old rookie, has hit just .201/.255/.332 (64 wRC+), and Meyers sustained a season-ending left kneecap injury at Triple-A Sugar Land last week.
Yet another injury-related note for the Red Sox: Ceddanne Rafaela was sidelined nearly three weeks ago due to a right quad strain. Prior to that, he was putting the finishing touches on a breakout season, having hit .282/.317/.443 (108 wRC+) with 16 homers and 17 steals while playing Gold Glove-caliber defense in center field. Less than a week after he went down, his capable fill-in Eli White suffered a ligament injury in his right foot, requiring season-ending surgery. Since then, Jarren Duran and Nate Eaton have shared the position. Rafaela has yet to return to the roster, though manager Chad Tracy said he’s “getting close.” If he does suffer a setback, continuing to play Duran during what’s been an awful season (.204/.261/.362, 68 wRC+) would obviously be less than ideal.
The Yankees’ Trent Grisham was sidelined by a Grade 2 strain of his right hamstring around the same time that Rafaela went down, and he has yet to return as well. His performance has fallen off drastically after a career year; he’s hit just .211/.308/.395 (98 wRC+) with 18 homers while trading some power for contact, and his defense has also been rough (-5 FRV and -8 DRS in 961.1 innings). While Boone has said he could be “in play at some point” during the postseason, there’s little urgency. Rookie Spencer Jones has shifted over from right field and done an impressive job of holding down the fort, playing adequate defense while hitting .246/.316/.435 (110 wRC+) despite a 36.2% strikeout rate.
Right Field: Heliot Ramos and Aaron Judge, Yankees
Yes, that looks weird in print, but for the moment at least, it’s a reality for the Yankees. The 27-year-old Ramos hit a modest .264/.304/.424 (100 wRC+) with nine homers and 0.6 WAR for the Giants before being traded to the Yankees on August 3. He began his time in pinstripes by going 5-for-47, and at one point went 32 games between homers — from July 20 to August 29 — while slugging .204. He’s heated up since then, but his .168/.294/.356 (85 wRC+) line with the Yankees doesn’t give anyone much confidence he can replace even the banged-up version of Judge the Yankees have received in his 66 games this season (.241/.360/.511, 141 wRC+).
In terms of concerns about sheer replacement-level production, the White Sox stand out here. Early in the season, the team tried Everson Pereira, Jarred Kelenic, and Rikuu Nishida as their regular at the position, but none got the job done. On June 9 they called up Braden Montgomery, a switch-hitting 23-year-old who placed 100th on our Top 100 as a 50-FV prospect in the spring. He collected two hits in his debut that night against the Braves, capped by a walk-off homer, but it’s been mostly downhill since then, as he’s hit .212/.305/.340 (84 wRC+) with six homers and 0.5 WAR in 88 games. While he’s hit .248/.344/.385 (110 wRC+) in 250 plate appearances against righties, he’s flailed away at a .125/.204/.2227 clip in 98 plate appearances against lefties. With resurgent lefty-masher Randal Grichuk on the roster and hitting .331/.372/.650 (182 wRC+) in 172 plate appearances against lefties, there’s no reason that should be happening.
Designated Hitter: Andrew Benintendi, White Sox
No remaining AL contender ranks below 15th in the majors in wRC+ provided by their DHs, and the two lowest teams from among that subset, the Red Sox and Guardians, are respectively third and fourth in second-half wRC+ from that spot while using revolving casts of players. So I’m picking (on) Andrew Benintendi, who has hit a very modest .243/.302/.414 (98 wRC+) while starting at DH in 105 games, with Grichuk (19) the only other Chicago player in double digits. There’s nothing particularly terrible or mysterious about Benintendi’s performance, which beyond a September slump, has lined up with his expected stats quite well; he’s got 21st-percentile bat speed but a 66th-percentile squared-up rate and a 77th-percentile hard-hit rate. He doesn’t hit lefties (.227/.261/.250, 44 wRC+ in 47 PA this year), so manager Will Venable has either used Grichuk or one of his righty regulars there. For as impressive as the White Sox’s turnaround from three straight 100-loss seasons has been, you can see from this roundup that the team’s weaknesses have come to the fore as they’ve tried to sew up a playoff berth.

The Boston Red Sox clinched their second consecutive playoff berth Sunday and their third since 2021.
It was a season with the highest of highs and the lowest of lows in Boston as they started the season 10-17 before firing longtime manager Alex Cora.
In June, the Red Sox found themselves 14 games under .500 at a record of 32-46. This is when everything changed.
They swept the New York Yankees before losing two out of three games to the Washington Nationals.
The Red Sox went on the road and swept the Los Angeles Angels, Chicago White Sox and New York Mets to sit at 46-48 heading into the all-star break.
After nine straight road wins, the Red Sox headed home to face the 56-38 Tampa Bay Rays. Tampa has had Boston’s number in the past few seasons, but this weekend was different.
In the first game of a doubleheader after the break, the Red Sox took care of business 10-0. Then in the night cap, Tampa Bay Rays took an early 2-0 before outfielder Wilyer Abreu decided the next 24 hours were all about him. He hit two home runs on the way to a 5-3 Red Sox win.
The next game was the defining game of the winning streak. The Rays were matching the Sox in scoring all-game before Abreu stepped to the plate down 6-5 in the seventh. Abreu crushed a two-run homer to right field, sending himself and Fenway Park into a frenzy. His fourth home run in 24 hours put Boston up 7-6, a lead they would hold for 12 consecutive wins.
They swept Tampa the next day before taking the first two games of the series versus the Orioles to tie a franchise record 15 straight wins. That first win did not come without drama. A back-and-forth game was knotted up in the eighth when Caleb Durbin smacked a game winning homerun to left field. The “Durbinator” had a rough start to the season but became one of the centerpieces of this win streak.
The streak would end at 15 but just a week later, Boston would rip off another nine straight wins. Durbin hit a walk-off single in an instant classic 12-11 victory against the White Sox. Ceddanne Rafaela became the king of LA for a few days after smacking four home runs in three games against the back-to-back champs.
So here we are, the Red Sox are 84-72 with a firm grip on the second wild card spot in the American League. Now, the New York Yankees stand in their way.
The Yankees beat the Red Sox 2-1 in the three-game wildcard series last year, and Boston is looking for revenge this season.
The pitching will be the key for both teams. Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez will toe the rubber for Boston against the Yankees’ Gerritt Cole, Max Fried and Massachusetts’ own Cam Schlittler in the series.
In his first full season in the MLB, Tolle hit his stride. The southpaw posted a 3.02 ERA and a 10.4 K/9. He is also peaking at the right time, sporting a 0.75 ERA in two starts during September.
In a complete 180 from Tolle, Gray has been dominant in what may be his swan song in the majors. After being acquired via trade in the offseason, Gray has won 17 games, a career high for the veteran. He pitched 7.1 innings of one hit baseball while striking out nine in a June win over the Yankees.
Suarez signed a 5-year $130 million dollar contract with Boston in the offseason and has been solid as a member of the Sox. However, the 2026 all-star struggled in all three of his starts against the Yankees. The Bronx Bombers were 3-0 against Suarez.
Despite great performances by the Yankees, Suarez is a playoff pitcher. He had a 1.48 ERA in 42.2 postseason innings as a member of the Philadelphia Phillies. In Philadelphia’s 2022 run to the World Series, the Phillies won all five games Suarez pitched in. He only allowed two earned runs in 14.2 innings pitched in 2022.
Along with the starters, the back of the bullpen has been nails for Boston. Erik Miller, Garrett Whitlock and Aroldis Chapman handled the seventh, eighth and ninth innings for interim manager Chad Tracy and the Red Sox. Miller came over at the trade deadline and did not allow an earned run in his first 10 appearances. Whitlock has been a staple in the Red Sox bullpen since 2021 and is possibly having his best year yet. He has a 1.75 ERA in 53 appearances. Chapman continues to age like fine wine. The 38-year-old was named an all-star for the second straight year and is 34/36 in save situations this year.
The rest of the hitters for the Red Sox will need to do some heavy lifting if they want to compete with the Yankees. Boston acquired Adley Rutschman at the deadline, and the catcher will be required to switch hit and catch in the playoffs. The final week of the MLB season always features plenty of altered and adjusted pitching plans.
Normally the one consistent throughout the drumbeat of the 162-game MLB season is a team’s pitching plan; regardless of whether a team has an ace on the mound or is going with pitching madness, the goal is always to get the best position to win while taking it a day at a time.
But that's a bit different this week.
While some teams are playing out the string and giving their starters one last opportunity to pitch before drifting off into the winter, the teams that have already clinched are stuck in the limbo of trying to cover the now while also preparing for the postseason.
It’s not like football or basketball where you can just throw random backups out there. Every inning needs to be covered, and there’s only so many innings you can give to pitchers who aren’t a part of your postseason plans.
Even if the Guardians won’t be in that position for a couple days (even if they clinch a postseason spot later today the American League Central race still won’t be settled, the Boston Red Sox's already know their postseason fate by virtue of being all but locked into the American League’s No. 5 seed.
We got an early example of how that could change their pitching plans on Monday when manager Andy Tracy pulled budding ace Peyton Tolle after five innings, and we got another example of it later in the game whenTracy went to Erik Miller in the ninth inning of a tied game instead of going to Aroldis Chapman… and Miller gave up the go-ahead run on a Nathaniel Lowe sacrifice fly.
The Red Sox are already playing with their postseason plans in mind, and those plans just got a bit more convoluted thanks to Miller’s rough outing.
The Red sox's bullpen struggles could help the Guardians in their quest to make the postseason
While Miller has largely been excellent since the Red Sox acquired him in August, he’s now allowed a run in three straight appearances and seems to be falling down manager Andy Tracy’s trust tree.
Miller opened his outing by hitting Chase DeLauter on the forearm with a pitch before surrendering a single to Jo Adell that was followed by Lowe’s sacrifice fly.
After the game, Tracy said that Miller was “working through some things,” which was obvious to everyone in the ballpark and watching at home.
Those struggles set up what should be an interesting last two games at Fenway Park. The Sox have two of their best pitchers going in the final two games of the series (Sonny Gray today and Ranger Suarez tomorrow), and it’s hard to believe the Red Sox are going to give them a ton of run in either of their starts.
While the Guardians may not get a chance to benefit from Boston’s relief struggles in the postseason since Boston will likely be locked into the other side of the bracket, they can use it to their benefit over the next 48 hours as they work to nail down a postseason spot.

If you sign a pitcher to a $130 million contract, you're an MLB decision-maker (Hello! Hire me! I have good ideas and work fairly hard!) If you're not an MLB decision-maker and have the capacity to read my first sentence without taking it literally, you'll want that $130 million pitcher to pitch in big games. The Boston Red Sox signed Ranger Suarez to a 5-year, $130 million contract shortly after losing Alex Bregman to the Chicago Cubs this offseason.
Suarez wasn't making top dollar over the first eight years of his career, but he was pitching in big games. He threw in 11 postseason games for the Philadelphia Phillies, posting a 1.48 ERA on his way to four wins and one save. With one week remaining in the regular season, Suarez is lined up to start game three of the Wild Card series, although Chad Tracy said not to read into that yet. Despite Tracy's guidance, I'm choosing to read into it.
Suarez has been streaky this season. He posted a 2.10 ERA over five starts in June. In August, he registered a 5.70 ERA. If you believe in pitcher streakiness, you'll be pleased to know the lefty has allowed just two earned runs over his last three starts (19.2 innings). Is this the start of a hot streak, or just some fortunate outcomes over a short sample? To quote the owl from the Tootsie Pop commercial, let's find out!
Suarez is typically effective against lefties, although he hit some blips during the middle of the season. He sees mostly right-handed hitters, though the Yankees are likely to keep both Ben Rice and Cody Bellinger in the lineup, as well as potentially Austin Wells and Jazz Chisholm. When Suarez got into trouble against lefties this season, it was primarily by missing the edge of the zone too often, falling behind in counts, and walking hitters. In August, he walked 15% of the lefties he faced. In September, he's only seen 28 lefties, but he's dialed it in.
Suarez has simplified his approach, increasing his sinker and slider usage. He's thrown the sinker on the arm side where it can jam hitters, rather than trying to back door it.
His slider was also located low and on the glove side, which translated to a 50% chase rate. Suarez also increased his first-pitch strike percentage from 55% in August to 68% in September. When Suarez is ahead, hitters are forced to swing at more pitches on the edges, and it translates to easy outs. Bellinger and Rice both hit pitches on the inside part of the plate well. In a few meetings this season, Suarez has opted to pitch primarily away from them. If Suarez does pitch against the Yankees, it will be interesting to see if he tries to jam them or continues to pitch away. Either way, his sinker/slider combination has been very effective over the past few weeks.
Righties are the bigger question for Suarez. Fortunately, the Yankees' right-handed hitters without Aaron Judge in the lineup aren't as daunting. Paul Goldschmidt and Heliot Ramos are the two biggest names, while George Lombard has also hit lefties well in his debut season. Ramos and Lombard each have plenty of strikeouts in their game, as does Jose Caballero. Amed Rosario is also often in the lineup against lefties, but he's posted a wRC+ of just 6 — yes, you read that correctly — 6 against lefties over the past two months.
Back to Suarez. Over his last three starts, he's held righties to a .190 batting average while striking out 24.5% of them. He made some notable changes to his approach as well. He's made changes to both his usage rates and how he's deployed them.
For most of the season, he's led with his cutter against righties. It's been effective, as he's thrown it high and inside where it can jam hitters. In September, he's backed off the usage and thrown it more on the arm side. The strike rate has fallen, but the different approach might be helping his other pitches be more effective.
He's made up for the lower cutter usage by increasing his sinkers to righties. Here's a look at the heat map for most of the season and September.
Early in the season, he almost exclusively kept his sinker away from righties. More recently, he's used the whole plate, throwing it down and away as well as inside. The strike rate is up, while the contact against it is weak. With the cutter more on the arm side, it might be more difficult for hitters to pull the trigger on the sinker, leading to an increase in called strikes.
The other notable change Suarez has made is slashing his changeup usage. For much of his career, his changeup has been his best pitch against righties. The swinging strike rate has been between 15 and 20%, with weak contact against it. This season, the zone rate and chase rate are below his usual marks, leading to a strike rate below 50%. From the beginning of the season through the end of August, the pitch accounted for 17% of his offerings to righties. Over his last three starts, he's used the pitch just 8% of the time. He's thrown it in just four two-strike counts in September, despite it being his second most used pitch against righties for most of the season. While it's a good pitch when it's working, it hasn't been a weapon for most of this season.
Suarez's deep arsenal means it can look very different for him on a given day. After returning from injury in July, he used five pitches over 14% of the time. As the Red Sox inched closer to securing a playoff spot, he cut the changeup and covered that portion of the plate with a sinker. It's an approach that's worked, but could be exposed as hitters are more ready for it. While most of the games this week are largely meaningless, how Suarez approaches righties in his final start of the season is something to watch, and could be a tell for how he performs in the playoffs.

Garrett Crochet ruined Game 1 for the AL Wild Card series last year for the Yankees.
And he could be looking to inflict damage on Boston’s AL East rivals once again.
The sidelined lefty ace said he hit 96 mph in a live batting practice session Tuesday and believes he can contribute in the postseason.
“The way that … just went, I could go get outs,” Crochet said, according to the Boston Globe. “It depends obviously what role they want me in. It’s not really for me to say. I know myself and I know my body, and the biggest thing was that I felt good out there. Felt like I was able to ramp up intensity to a place that I haven’t gone yet. Tomorrow is going to be a big deal, seeing how I recover.”
The Yankees and Red Sox are seemingly on a collision course for a second straight Wild Card clash, although Boston has yet to secure the No. 5 seed.
The loser of the AL Central battle between the Guardians and White Sox can still overtake Boston for that date in The Bronx next Tuesday.
Boston entered last postseason with Crochet anchoring its rotation off a season that earned him second place in the AL Cy Young voting but question marks in the rotation after him.
This time around, Boston has established starters but Crochet is the question mark.
Crochet is closing in on five months since he last pitched in an MLB game after landing on the injured list in April with left shoulder inflammation, having last started April 25.
He did not pitch up to his standards in his six outings before being sidelined, posting a 6.30 ERA while allowing 33 hits and five homers in just 30 innings.
It’s uncertain how Boston would use him in the postseason due to the long layoff and the team having quality starters.
Lefties Peyton Tolle, Ranger Suarez and Jake Bennett plus righty Sonny Gray give Boston four capable starters to match up with the Yankees.
Last season, Crochet dominated the Yankees in Game 1, striking out 11 while allowing just one run in 7 2/3 innings in Boston’s 3-1 victory.
Brayan Bello lasted just 2 1/3 innings in a Game 2 loss and rookie Connelly Early logged only 3 2/3 innings in the decisive Game 3 loss.
“He’s definitely making progress,” Boston manager Chad Tracy — fresh off his promotion to full-time skipper — said, per the Boston Globe. “Again, it’s ‘see how he feels tomorrow.’ I know that there’s a lot of conversation around that because we’re only a week away from the postseason now. So determining how does he feel coming out of that [and] what does this weekend look like is going to be the next step.
“What that looks like now, I don’t know. I just know that whatever it is, it’s going to be done with Garrett’s best interest in mind, making sure that we’re doing it right.”
Crochet noted that he would “feel bad” taking someone’s spot on the roster, and said he would accept whatever the front office decides.
With the season ending Sunday, Boston does not have any soft landing spots to allow Crochet to face major-league hitters in a true game environment before the playoffs begin.
Boston ultimately may just have to trust that its star pitcher can return with no hiccups.
“You’re considering all those things,” Tracy said, per the Boston Globe. “We have to consider it and just be very, very mindful of, again, what are we potentially exposing him to and what can he give us really?”

item.content:encoded:
The Craig Breslow era in Boston has felt like a roller coaster ride. Hired at the start of the 2023-24 offseason, the Boston Red Sox have not had a losing season under Breslow, despite wild swings in the team's form over the three years.
With the Red Sox clinching a playoff berth for the second year in a row, team ownership decided that now was the time to exercise two options on their Chief Baseball Officer's contract, guaranteeing his deal for the 2029 and 2030 seasons. On the surface, a head of baseball operations who got his team to the playoffs in years two and three of their time running the club getting years added to their contract, would make sense, but in Breslow's case it isn't as straightforward.
It was only three months ago when most of Red Sox Nation was calling for Breslow's head. The Red Sox were 32-46 on June 24, dead last in the division, and it already seemed like the season was over. It took a miraculous turnaround to get the team to the playoffs. Not to say that Breslow had nothing to do with that; he had added a lot of players to the roster who were key contributors, but that has a lot more to do with the players and coaches than the front office.
Breslow's tenure has also been marred by controversy, specifically the Rafael Devers drama. It was his handling of the situation, along with former manager Alex Cora, that ultimately led to the fracture of the relationship with the team's then-face of the franchise. While the fanbase was split on whose side they took, player or team, his actions after the fact didn't make it any better.
Red Sox's Craig Breslow had the hottest seat of any GM only three months ago
It was the signing of Alex Bregman that caused the Devers drama in the first place. While Breslow was praised for the signing, Bregman opted out at the end of the year and was then not re-signed. The Red Sox went from two elite third basemen to none in the span of a season. It wasn't a good look for the Red Sox CBO.
Now, Breslow's pivot from all of the drama and mess surrounding Devers and Bregman looks incredibly good in hindsight. The additions of Ranger Suarez, Sonny Gray, Willson Contreras, Caleb Durbin, and others have been extremely impactful to the Red Sox's success this season. While some of those moves were celebrated at the time they happened, others like the Durbin-Kyle Harrison swap (that also netted the Red Sox Andruw Monasterio and Anthony Seigler) were heavily scrutinized.
Breslow also made good moves at the trade deadline, adding Erik Miller and Eli White, who have looked good for the Sox. He also made the splash trade for Adley Rutschman, which hasn't worked as well on the field, but certainly instilled confidence in the team, knowing the front office believed in them.
Red Sox could've softened the impact by extending one of Craig Breslow's options at first
All of this is to say that Breslow's time as CBO hasn't been as smooth sailing as the records would suggest. He has had some high highs but also some low lows. Why did ownership feel the need to exercise both options right now? The first option wasn't needed until the 2029 season, two years out. The second was for 2030, three years out.
Doing the first one now would've been fine — picking up the 2029 option gives Breslow another three comfortable seasons on his contract. That would make him more comfortable making moves for the future and give him the job security to know he will likely be in place to see them play out. Selecting the 2030 option on the same day was unnecessary, though.
There have been too many hiccups in the three years under Breslow to say he has warranted another four seasons. The start of 2026 could easily repeat itself in 2027. Should ownership feel the need to relieve him of his duties early, then this makes it that much harder. Breslow hasn't won a World Series in Boston; in fact, he hasn't even made it out of the Wild Card round. Exercising the option for 2030 feels very premature.
Breslow has not done a bad job in Boston. At the end of the day, it's results that matter, and Breslow's teams have made the playoffs two out of three times. He shouldn't be fearing for his job, but his contract also wasn't ending for another two seasons. It feels early to be handing him the keys so far down the road after the drama of his first two years as CBO.

item.content:encoded:
The postseason begins on September 29, giving teams one day of rest between the end of the regular season and the start of the race. Playoff teams must plan their rotations early have the right pitchers rested and ready for the opening series and the Boston Red Sox have seemingly made their call.
The Red Sox's rotation for their upcoming matchup with the Cleveland Guardians, their second-to-last series of the year, is Payton Tolle in game one, Sonny Gray in game two and Ranger Suarez in game three. That leaves Patrick Sandoval, Jake Bennett and Brayan Bello (or a bullpen game) for the final series against the Chicago Cubs, not necessarily in that order.
Tolle has earned the series-opening start against the New York Yankees. He's posted a 2.36 ERA and 0.88 WHIP with 56 strikeouts over his last seven starts. He's stayed hot despite having 143 innings on his arm this year, and he's gotten even better as the year has gone on.
Tolle has had previous success against the Yankees, including two stellar outings this year. He faced the Yankees in his first big league appearance this year and allowed just one run on three hits with 11 strikeouts and a walk over six innings. Tolle next faced New York on June 26 (one of the games in the four-game sweep that started Boston's historic summer winning streak) and he pitched seven, one-hit innings with seven strikeouts.
Red Sox-Guardians series likely previews Boston's Wild Card rotation with Payton Tolle starting Game 1
Starting Tolle first could set up a battle between two young lefties and Cy Young Award contenders (though it isn't much of a contest) if the Yankees plan to open the series with their ace Cam Schlittler. This might not be the case, though, as New York seems to be setting Gerrit Cole up for the Game 1 start. The Red Sox don't fare as well against right-handed pitching as they do against lefties, with a .712 team OPS against them, and taking Boston off its game will be a high priority for its rival.
Whether the Red Sox win or lose Game 1, Game 2 means everything. With a series loss or a sweep on the line, Boston's ace Gray should take the mound. The 36-year-old Gray has surprised fans everywhere by posting one of the best seasons of his career with the Red Sox and his consistency is unmatched.
Gray has clocked a 2.82 ERA, 1.16 WHIP, 146 strikeouts and 45 walks over 163 innings. Like the Red Sox, the Yankees also don't perform especially well against righty pitching, with a .713 OPS as a club. With a sweep on the line or to stay alive, the veteran Gray is the guy to trust.
In a win-or-go-home Game 3, Suarez deserves Boston's trust. He's gotten back on his feet over the last few weeks following a shaky spell (5.70 ERA in August) after a groin injury. Postseason starts are Suarez's bread and butter — he boasts a 1.48 ERA and 1.06 WHIP over 42.2 frames across seven playoff series — and he's the best choice to keep the Red Sox alive when they're on the brink of elimination.
Boston's rotation has been the biggest strength of the team all season. With these three pitchers, in any order, the Red Sox have good chances to get past the Yankees to advance to the Division Series. But setting the energy with Tolle and having the two veterans follow, as Boston has set things up, makes a lot of sense.

With just a few games remaining in the regular season, the chances of a Red Sox vs. Yankees matchup in the AL Wild Card round appear high.
If the Rays can officially clinch the AL East, and the Red Sox can pull away from the White Sox for the AL's No. 5 seed, Boston will be traveling to face New York in a best-of-three matchup.
So when Aaron Boone announced the latest on Aaron Judge's injury status on Tuesday, it carried massive implications for the Red Sox as they begin looking toward the postseason.
Here's the latest on Judge and what it could mean for the Red Sox.
How Yankees' Aaron Judge Injury Update Affects Red Sox
On Tuesday, Boone told reporters that Judge, who was recently played on the 10-day IL with a calf strain just days after his return from a significant injury, is dealing with a "moderate grade" strain.
However, more significantly, Boone said the Yankees aren't preparing for Judge to be ready for the start of the postseason after he had a PPP injection on Monday.
"We’re planning on him not being a part of that,” Boone said, per Bryan Hoch.
While Judge's status for a likely wild-card matchup won't become official until early next week, when the Yankees would have to finalize their roster for a series, it's looking unlikely that he will be healthy in time.
For the Red Sox, no Judge would change the dynamic of attacking the Yankees' lineup. While Ben Rice and Cody Bellinger remain power threats themselves, the presence of the three-time AL MVP boosts New York's offense to an elite status. Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez and Payton Tolle — likely to pitch for Boston in a best-of-three series — wouldn't have to worry about the threat of Judge's bat breaking a game open in one swing.
Red Sox vs. Yankees is not yet official, and neither is Judge's status for the postseason. But as of Tuesday, all indications are that New York will have to host Boston without its superstar outfielder.

After a rollercoaster of a season which included a brutal start, sudden managerial firings, historic win streaks and a playoff clinch, the Boston Red Sox have extended the man who brought it all together. Boston has removed Chad Tracy's "interim" tag and made him their manager, first reported by Christopher Smith of MassLive.
Tracy and the Red Sox have agreed to a three-year contract with a club option in 2030, per Smith. His salary has not yet been reported.
Tracy was Boston's Triple-A manager on April 25, the day Alex Cora and six other members of his coaching staff were fired. The Red Sox then flew him out to Baltimore to take over in a whirlwind and a leap of faith, and it worked. He'll be the 49th manager in Red Sox franchise history (subscription required).
The Red Sox had a 10-17 record on the day of Tracy's promotion and he managed the club to two games below .500 by July 12, the start of the All-Star break. Boston's historic 15-game winning streak had already begun by then — it rallied to sweep the New York Yankees in four games two weeks before, lost a series to the Washington Nationals, and it was all winning from there.
Red Sox name Chad Tracy manager through 2029, exercised club options to keep Craig Breslow CBO through 2030
Tracy had long been revered as the manager of the WooSox and it didn't take long for Red Sox fans to become equally endeared to him. His direct, but friendly communication style offered a stark contrast to other leaders in the organization. He had preexisting relationships with many of the organization's young players from their time in Triple-A and from rehab assignments, and it showed. After the Red Sox's historic July and August spell, Tracy's promotion seemed almost inevitable, and rightfully so.
Within the Tracy contract announcement, the Red Sox also included another contract update. The Red Sox have exercised the 2029-30 club options on Craig Breslow's contract, essentially extending him for another two years.
This is quite a sign of trust from Boston. Breslow's tenure started with some massive moves like the Garrett Crochet trade, and the Red Sox made the playoffs for the first time in three seasons with him at the helm. But his communication style has been criticized, it's led to massive trades of players who were supposed to be fixtiures of the organization for years to come, and front office leaks have marred his public image.
But Breslow has loosened up a bit since the beginning of the season. He's been pictured around the players more often and has been cracking jokes on his radio appearances.
There's also no denying that he had a great 2025-26 offseason. Sonny Gray, Willson Contreras, Ranger Suarez and Caleb Durbin, all acquired by Breslow over the offseason, are all major parts of the Red Sox's success.
Cora had been Boston's manager for eight seasons and many Red Sox fans couldn't stand Breslow at the beginning of June. Things can change quickly in baseball.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox have scored 2.82 runs per game across their last 11 outings. The lineup is collectively batting .210 and posting a .621 OPS in that span. Wilyer Abreu, Adley Rutschman, Isiah Kiner-Falefa, and Nick Sogard have all gone cold at the wrong time.
With the Wild Card Series beginning September 29, the Red Sox need their bats to wake up before October arrives.
The cavalry is coming. And the timing could not be better.
The Latest on Rafaela
Ceddanne Rafaela is expected to return to the lineup on Tuesday when the Red Sox open a three-game series against the Guardians at Fenway Park.
The All-Star center fielder has been sidelined for 16 games since straining his right quadriceps.
Chad Tracy indicated over the weekend that Rafaela should come off the injured list for the homestand. The rotation is set up with Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez, a sequence that mirrors how the staff could be deployed in the Wild Card Series.
Getting Rafaela back before those games begin gives him a chance to find his timing and reintegrate into the lineup before the stakes get higher.
What Rafaela Brings Back
Rafaela's absence has been felt. On the season, he has produced 16 home runs, 70 RBIs, and a .282/.760 line. His combination of contact, power, and speed makes him one of the most complete players on the roster.
The defensive impact is equally significant. Rafaela's range in center field changes the way the pitching staff operates. Fly balls that fall for hits with other outfielders become outs when he is patrolling the middle of the outfield. His presence there tightens the entire defense.
The Red Sox have been using Jarren Duran and Nate Eaton to fill the void in center. Both have been serviceable, but neither provides the combination of offense and defense that Rafaela delivers on a daily basis.
The Red Sox Offense Needs a Spark
The numbers paint a clear picture of how badly the Red Sox have struggled at the plate.
Mickey Gasper is 4-for-25 over the recent stretch. Kiner-Falefa has managed just one hit in his last 20 at-bats. Sogard is 8-for-40. The lineup has lacked the consistent production that fueled the summer surge.
There have been bright spots. Roman Anthony broke out of a prolonged slump with a 5-for-13 weekend against the Rays that included two doubles and a homer. Trevor Story has been one of the hottest hitters on the roster since returning from the injured list, carrying a .338 average with an .869 OPS across 19 games.
Willson Contreras is also working his way back from a bruised right hand and could return this week. If both Contreras and Rafaela rejoin the lineup for the Guardians series, it would be the healthiest the Red Sox' batting order has looked in weeks.
Final Word for the Red Sox
The Red Sox have six games left before the playoffs begin.
Rafaela's return gives the lineup a jolt it needs. What he provides on both sides of the ball is invaluable for Boston.
Fenway awaits.

item.content:encoded:
Ranger Suarez is back to having fun after clinching the playoffs. Despite losing on Sunday, the Boston Red Sox clinched their spot in the postseason due to other teams' losses. The Sox took a team picture on the field at Tropicana Field before heading into the clubhouse for the usual champagne showers and beer.
In the team photo, Suarez clearly sticks out. Standing right in the middle, the lefty starter had bright red shorts pulled up well above his waist, and his celebratory shirt tucked in. He was also the only player in the picture with his goggles already covering his eyes. Suarez was known as a fun celebration guy with the Philadelphia Phillies, and it was something the fans there loved about him; Red Sox Nation was just waiting to see in Boston.
While Suarez is all fun and games with good spirits during a celebration, he does a complete 180 once the playoffs start. He's been one of the best playoff pitchers ever. His 1.48 ERA is the sixth-lowest of all time among pitchers with at least 40 innings pitched in the playoffs.
The 31-year-old has pitched in each of the last four postseasons. In 2023, he allowed just two earned runs in 14 2/3 innings. In 2024, he allowed four earned runs in 18 2/3 innings. In 2024, he allowed no runs in 4 1/3 innings. In 2025, he allowed one earned run in five innings. In the regular season, the lefty has a career 8.4 K/9; in the playoffs, it's 9.3
Ranger Suarez's playoff pedigree should excite fans after last season's playoff rotation
His playoff excellence was part of the reason the Red Sox signed him. While Suarez has been a very solid regular-season pitcher, it was his success in the playoffs that really made him stand out in last season's free-agent pool. After Garrett Crochet, the Red Sox ended up relying on Brayan Bello and Connelly Early. The Sox knew they needed another playoff-tested arm for the postseason and made the splash signing of the lefty to do so.
The Red Sox now head into the 2026 playoffs with a projected Wild Card round rotation that will consist of Suarez, Sonny Gray, and Payton Tolle. While the exact order is yet to be determined, those three arms will instill much more confidence than the three who started the games last year.
Suarez likes to have his fun. He did so in Philly and is doing so again here in Boston. That doesn't mean that opponents should take him lightly. Come playoff time, Suarez turns it on and shuts down the other teams.
