item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox are officially headed back to the postseason, and by clinching a spot with more than a week to spare, the club now has the luxury of making all of its playoff preparations without stressing about the final six-game homestand.
But there’s still unfinished business to attend to, so here are a few loose threads the Red Sox need to address before Game 1 of the American League Wild Card Series next Tuesday.
Who starts Game 1?
When the Red Sox return to Fenway Park for this week’s penultimate series against the Cleveland Guardians, they will send Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez to the mound, in that order.
Could that be a preview of the AL Wild Card Series rotation? Maybe, but not necessarily.
It’s a testament to the season Tolle has enjoyed that he’s a realistic choice to start Game 1. The rookie left-hander has been fantastic all season, posting a 3.02 ERA over 143 innings through 25 starts, and he’s been especially impressive as the season has gone along.
Gray and Suarez are obviously the more experienced options, but if Tolle is capable of delivering a shutdown playoff performance like Garrett Crochet last fall, there’s merit in sending him out as soon as possible rather than waiting for a do-or-die Game 3 scenario.
If not Tolle, Gray is the obvious choice to start Game 1. Gray has been the ace of the staff ever since Crochet went down in April, and starting the veteran right off the bat would also allow the Red Sox to throw Tolle or Suarez on extra rest no matter which order they chose.
Bello or Bennett as long man?
If there’s a player whose individual season best parallels the 2026 Red Sox, it might be Brayan Bello.
Coming into the year as one of Boston’s longest-tenured starters, Bello completely imploded and lost not just his spot in the Red Sox rotation but his place on the big league roster entirely. But since returning from Triple-A just before the All-Star break, Bello has been fantastic, and last time out he delivered one of the best starts of his career, striking out 11 over eight dominant innings.
Between that and another strong showing against the Angels earlier this month, it appears Bello has finally gotten past whatever issues he was having in the first inning early on. Given that Jake Bennett has been a bit shaky recently, the Red Sox may need to consider the possibility that Bello might actually be the club’s best option as the No. 4 starter should the Red Sox advance to the ALDS.
But there are other factors to consider, too.
With the club only needing three starters for the best-of-three Wild Card series, it would make sense for the Red Sox to leave their No. 4 starter off the wild card roster so they can be lined up and fresh for Game 1 of the ALDS. Since Bennett has never pitched out of the bullpen in his MLB career, and Bello has proven quite adept in that role, it would make sense to stick with Bennett as the No. 4 starter and roster Bello as the long man.
But on the flip side, carrying three starters means the Red Sox won’t need a No. 5 starter either, which means they can add a ninth short-inning reliever on top of the long-man. With all hands on deck and presumably Tolle, Gray and Suarez capable of going deep into the game, the Red Sox could prioritize keeping the preferred Game 1 ALDS starter in reserve, in which case having Bennett as the emergency arm wouldn’t be the end of the world.
Will any rehabbing arms make roster?
With extra spots in the bullpen up for grabs, the Red Sox have to decide if any of their rehabbing arms have progressed to a point where they’re a better option than some of the club’s lower-leverage relievers.
Tanner Houck seems to be the most likely candidate for a bullpen spot at this point. He’s made four appearances out of the bullpen in the minors since the start of September, alternating between 20-pitch short outings and 40-pitch bulk appearances. With the minor league season over and a playoff spot clinched, it wouldn’t be a surprise to see Houck activated this week to pitch in the final homestand, which would both allow the clubs higher leverage arms to stay fresh and potentially serve as a playoff audition for Houck.
How about Crochet? He would almost certainly be limited to one inning at a time, but he also hasn’t faced live hitters yet. If Crochet throws live batting practice this week and comes out looking good, it’s possible the Red Sox could make a bet on his immense upside, though, if the club is serious about not rushing him back it might make sense to hold off until at least the ALDS.
Two longer-shot candidates that can’t be completely ruled out are Johan Oviedo and Kutter Crawford. Oviedo made his first in-game appearance since March last week, throwing 2 1/3 innings for the WooSox in a rehab outing, and Crawford was scheduled to pitch Sunday’s season finale for Worcester before that game was rained out. It would be a surprise if either factors into the playoff picture, but they could conceivably make cameos in Boston this week to help cover some innings down the stretch.
Who will be last man on bench?
The Red Sox are going to have to make some tough decisions when it comes to constructing their bench. Assuming the club carries a back-up catcher — probably Connor Wong — they’ll only have three additional spots and more than a half dozen candidates to fill them.
For starters, which of Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Andruw Monasterio or Romy Gonzalez will serve as the primary back-up right-handed infielder. Would the Red Sox carry two of the three? Or just one to make room for Jahmai Jones as the lefty-killing pinch hitter and emergency outfielder?
How about Mickey Gasper? He’s been one of the club’s best hitters since mid-August and would provide a potent left-handed weapon to use in a late-inning spot against a big righty reliever.
And lastly, do the Red Sox reserve a spot for a dedicated pinch runner like Dave Roberts back in 2004? If so, then maybe Braiden Ward, who just stole 61 bases for the WooSox, might have a chance to make his MLB debut in the playoffs.
Will Mother Nature throw a curveball?
Before the Red Sox even get to the playoffs, they may have to navigate a messy weather situation.
As of this writing, the forecasts indicate a nor’easter could bring heavy rain, gusty winds and coastal flooding to the Boston area throughout the weekend. That is not conducive to playing outdoor baseball, and while the Red Sox probably won’t have anything to play for, the series could have big ramifications for the Chicago Cubs and the National League Wild Card race.
Could the Red Sox wind up having to play a Monday doubleheader to complete the 162-game schedule? MLB will surely do everything it can to avoid that, but the league will be watching the weather closely over the next few days.

item.content:encoded:
Jesús David Castellano / @_JDCastellano
Willson Contreras se convirtió en el líder espiritual de los Medias Rojas de Boston en lo que fue un camino transformador que pasó de una virtual catástrofe a la clasificación a postemporada por segundo año consecutivo.
Y es que tras finalizar la jornada del 17 de junio con récord de 29-42, los Medias Rojas ganaron 55 de sus siguientes 85 juegos —la mayor cantidad de todo el béisbol— para mejorar su foja a 84 victorias y 72 derrotas y sellar su boleto a playoffs el pasado domingo, luego de que los Bravos de Atlanta ayudaran venciendo a los Astros de Houston.
Los Medias Rojas no pudieron celebrar con un triunfo en el bolsillo. Cayeron ante Tampa Bay en el último de la serie en Tropicana Field, pero eso poco importó, sobre todo teniendo en cuenta todo el camino recorrido para anotar su nombre en la fiesta de octubre luego de estar destinados al desastre en los primeros tres meses de zafra. Sencillamente nunca se rindieron, y eso lo reconoce Willson y se lo hace ver a sus compañeros.
«Un año bastante bendecido y acontecido»
«Primeramente, darle las gracias a Dios por todo lo vivido este año. Un año bastante bendecido y acontecido», dijo Willson a El Extrabase durante la celebración en el clubhouse visitante del Tropicana Field. «También hay que agradecer por el equipo que tenemos alrededor, los muchachos, la clase de personas que tenemos. Y de verdad que nunca dejamos de trabajar, ni de perseguir ese cupo a los playoffs».
En un buen tramo de la campaña, el primera base carabobeño comandó a la ofensiva patirroja. Primeramente, despuntó bateando por encima de .300 en abril y luego mantuvo la constancia suficiente como para terminar encabezando al equipo —con seis compromisos por disputar en el calendario regular— en cuadrangulares (27), carreras impulsadas (81), porcentaje de embasado (.387), slugging (.518) y OPS (.905).
Su escolta en el renglón de vuelacercas fue Wilyer Abreu (24), que no solo aportó con el bate, sino con su prodigiosa defensa en los jardines que lo tiene como firme candidato a obtener su tercer guante de oro consecutivo.
Elogios para Abreu y Monasterio
«Estoy orgulloso de todos mis compañeros, especialmente de Wilyer; por todo lo que ha hecho este año y lo que ha logrado, ha sido bastante importante, igual que (Andruw) Monasterio, que lo trajeron para acá a hacer un trabajo. Se amoldó muy bien a su rol y mira, esto es lo que hace un equipo unido, clasificar», añadió.
«Estoy verdaderamente orgulloso del equipo que formamos y que tenemos ahora mismo», acotó Wilyer, que comanda a los jardineros derechos de la Liga Americana en Carreras Salvadas a la Defensiva con 26. «Le dimos la vuelta a la temporada de una forma increíble. Me siento orgulloso de haber sido parte de esto, de poder ayudar y contribuir al equipo en este momento y durante toda la temporada».
Wilyer también destaca entre los jugadores de su posición en el nuevo circuito siendo segundo en Outs Por Encima del Promedio (3) y primero en valor en carreras de fildeo (5). Igualmente, despunta en asistencias desde los jardines (12) y en el apartado ofensivo, lidera a los Medias Rojas en carreras anotadas (81), dobles (36, con lo que comanda la Liga Americana) y bases por bolas (70). El zuliano estableció topes personales en las categorías ofensivas antes mencionadas, además de traídas al plato (74), imparables (144) y, por supuesto, bambinazos (24).
Monasterio ha entendido su rol
Por su parte, Andruw Monasterio supo adaptarse a su rol de pelotero de reemplazo, con tramos destacados a la ofensiva. Un ejemplo de ello fue julio. En ese entonces asumió la titularidad de las paradas cortas en ausencia del lesionado Trevor Story, lo que coincidió con la racha de 15 triunfos seguidos que le dio vida a Boston. Exhibió un promedio de .338 (de 65-22), OBP de .413, slugging de .631 y OPS de 1.044, con tres cuadrangulares, 11 producidas y nueve anotadas.
Pero no se limitó al campo corto; Monasterio también vio acción en segunda, en primera, e incluso en tercera.
«Para mí, todo fue amoldarme a mi rol», comentó Monasterio a El Extrabase. «Fui al Spring Training y me gané el puesto. Súper contento porque son cuatro años en el show y cuatro años clasificando, es una bendición. Es muy satisfactorio, porque tú trabajas mucho para esto, para este momento del año, el béisbol en octubre».
Suárez ha sido clave en el tramo final
En el renglón del pitcheo, Ranger Suárez ha sido clave en este tramo final de la zafra, luego de presentar altibajos durante gran parte del año e incluso estar en lista de lesionados después de la pausa del juego de estrellas.
En sus últimas cinco aperturas exhibe foja de 3-1 y una efectividad de 2.70 en 30 innings de labor, con 22 ponches, 12 pasaportes y un WHIP de 1.27. Todo eso ha confluido en una actuación general en su primera contienda en la Liga Americana, en la que posee un promedio de carreras limpias de 3.27 en 143.1 capítulos de trabajo a lo largo de 27 salidas.
«Contento del sacrificio que hicimos durante la temporada, especialmente por cómo empezamos», expresó el zurdo de Pie de Cuesta. «Entonces, mira lo que nos recompensó Dios, estamos en los playoffs».
A Ranger se lo ha caracterizado por ser un lanzador bastante calmado, casi imperturbable. Y bastante de eso mostró el equipo para lograr revertir su situación de inicio de temporada. «No comenzamos de la manera que queríamos, pero el talento de los muchachos es increíble. Sabíamos que le íbamos a dar vuelta a la situación».

The New York Yankees are almost guaranteed to face the Boston Red Sox in an upcoming best-of-three Wild Card series, and can lock up homefield advantage with either a singular win in their final seven games or one Boston loss. The time is now for forecasting and getting your ducks in a row, and the Yankees have acknowledged as such; resetting Brent Headrick, for example, is more important than going all out to embarrass the Tampa Bay Rays this week.
That makes every rotation decision or perceived pattern seem magnified, especially after Boston lined up their starters for their upcoming series with the Cleveland Guardians: Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, Ranger Suárez. Is that the chips falling where they may, or is that foreshadowing? Either way, while winking and nodding, it's probably time to read similarly into the way the Yankees are handlng things.
That's why our eyebrows raised on Sunday when the Yanks revealed that Cam Schlittler and Gerrit Cole will stay on turn in the Rays series (for now), with Schlittler closing the four-game set and Cole pitching Game 3, both staying out of the doubleheader. That will leave Cole with an extra day of rest ahead of the WIld Card opener and Schlittler on normal rest. You're not saying ... ?
All the love in the world to Gerrit Cole, who got closer to securing an all-important Wild Card Series start with his strong appearance in the desert on Friday night. But given that his spot in the rotation in general has been rightly questioned, there is no world where he should start Game 1 over Schlittler. That is not even something that should be rolling around in the canals of my addled gray brain. And yet!
Yankees giving Gerrit Cole the rest he needs ahead of Wild Card Series. Will Cam Schlittler even start vs. Rays?
For now, this is all hypothetical, but ... Cole has always seemed like a candidate for a deciding Game 3, but nothing before it. Would the Yankees really dare to use him in a deciding game with three extra days of rest building up on his right arm?
And, if the Rays clinch the AL East this week and the Yankees lock down their positioning, will they use Schlittler at all in this series? Will he make a perfunctory three-inning cameo just to keep his sea legs ahead of the Sox showdown and prevent overthrowing/overcompensating? The Cy Young race between he and Dylan Cease is informally over, and Cease may not even be healthy enough to make another start. If positioning gets more solidified throughout the week, these decisions only become more fascinating.
As of now, though, before any adjustments ... it seems like there's at least a chance the Yankees are lining up Cole for Game 1 - or working him out of the picture entirely.

The Boston Red Sox have officially clinched a postseason berth, completing one of the most improbable turnarounds in MLB history.
But the real test begins next week. After falling to the New York Yankees in last year’s Wild Card Series, Boston is looking to make a deeper October run this time around, and it looks like the Yankees will once again stand in the way.
It’s been a total team effort for Boston all season long, but the playoffs are where stars emerge and the margin for error becomes razor thin. While nearly everyone on the postseason roster will play a role, we’ve narrowed it down to the 10 players who could have the biggest impact on how far this team goes.
Here are the 10 most important -- not necessarily the best -- Red Sox players for the 2026 playoffs:
1. Payton Tolle, SP
What a difference a year makes. Last year, Tolle experienced growing pains in his first MLB stint and pitched just 1/3 of an inning in the Wild Card Series at Yankee Stadium. This time, he's coming off an exceptional rookie campaign with a chance to start Game 1 in the Bronx.
Tolle will enter the postseason with momentum on his side. The 23-year-old tallied 12 strikeouts while allowing just one run in six innings against Baltimore. He followed that up with six shutout innings against Kansas City, including an immaculate inning to begin the game.
If Tolle continues to perform at this level, he'll give the Red Sox another frontline starter who can match up against other teams' aces. He's the pitcher with the greatest opportunity to change the trajectory of this postseason roster.
If the Red Sox make a deep postseason run, it'll be because their rookie left-hander delivered each time he took the mound on the big stage.
2. Sonny Gray, SP
We're sticking with pitching, because pitching is what propelled this Red Sox club to a postseason berth in the first place.
If Tolle is No. 1, it would be silly not to put Gray right behind him at No. 2. The 36-year-old veteran stabilized the rotation in the wake of Garrett Crochet's injury. He was signed to be the No. 3 starter behind Crochet and Ranger Suarez, but he performed like an ace with a 17-5 record and a 2.82 ERA in 28 starts.
Now, Boston will lean on Gray and his big-game experience to lead the staff in October. Even if he doesn't start Game 1 of the Wild Card Series, Gray will play a huge role in any postseason success.
3. Roman Anthony, LF/DH
The top position player on our list is the 22-year-old many expected to anchor Boston's lineup and produce an MVP-caliber season in 2026. Instead, Anthony spent most of the year on the injured list and has largely struggled in the 50 games he's been healthy. We know what the former No. 1 prospect is capable of, however, and he'll significantly raise the Red Sox' ceiling if he plays up to his potential in the postseason.
The Red Sox will lean heavily on their pitching staff throughout the playoffs, but Anthony is the X-factor in the lineup. This is a completely different club when he gets hot.
All it will take is a signature postseason moment for Red Sox fans to forget about the disappointing start to Anthony's young career.
4. Ranger Suarez, SP
OK, back to pitching. A big reason the Red Sox signed Suarez to a five-year, $130 million contract in free agency is that he has a stellar postseason track record. The 31-year-old boasts a 1.48 ERA across 11 playoff appearances (eight starts) with the Philadelphia Phillies.
The only reason he isn't higher on this list is we project him to be the No. 3 starter, which means we won't even see him if the Sox get swept out of the Wild Card Series. If Boston advances, another strong postseason from Suarez will be critical for their World Series chances.
5. Wilyer Abreu, RF
Abreu is one of Boston's best all-around players, but he's a streaky hitter. The Red Sox' mediocre offense can't afford for him to go cold in the postseason, so he's an incredibly important piece if they hope to make a deep run.
When he's hot, Abreu's bat is elite. He leads the American League with 36 doubles along with 24 homers in 151 games.
As important as his bat will be, Abreu's Gold Glove defense in right field will also be a difference-maker. Postseason games can come down to one defensive miscue, and Abreu has earned a reputation as one of the best defensive right fielders in baseball.
If Abreu can give the Red Sox consistent at-bats and quality defense, he can quietly become one of the most impactful players on the roster over an entire series.
6. Willson Contreras, 1B
We've got the Venezuelan sluggers back-to-back. Contreras has been the Red Sox' most consistent bat all season, and he'll be leaned on heavily in the heart of the lineup throughout the playoffs.
Unlike most of Boston's lineup, Contreras will enter the Wild Card Series with plenty of postseason experience. He won a World Series with the 2016 Chicago Cubs and has 30 playoff games under his belt in total.
With a team-high 27 homers, Contreras will be counted on to supply the Red Sox lineup with power throughout their playoff run. If he goes cold, there will be even more pressure on guys like Anthony, Abreu, and the player who's next up on our list to get runs on the board.
7. Adley Rutschman, C
Rutschman will need to step it up offensively, but his importance goes beyond his bat because of his position. One could argue the role he plays behind the plate is even more crucial.
As Boston's starting catcher, Rutschman will be responsible for managing the pitching staff through almost every postseason game, meaning he'll be involved on almost every pitch thrown. There's also a significant downgrade at catcher if he goes down with an injury, with only Connor Wong and Mickey Gasper as his potential backups.
For the Red Sox to make it far, Rutschman has to be more than just a productive hitter; he must also work seamlessly with the rotation and bullpen while living up to his reputation as one of the best defensive backstops in the league.
8. Aroldis Chapman, CP
Having a closer who can slam the door shut gives clubs a huge advantage come postseason time. The Red Sox are fortunate to have arguably the best of the bunch.
While Chapman wasn't otherworldly in 2026 like he was in 2025, he still was elite with a 1.95 ERA in 52 appearances. He'll look to limit free passes after watching his walk rate jump from 2.2 to 4.1 BB/9 over last year. If he does that, Boston can effectively shorten games by having him available for the ninth inning. He can also single-handedly lose games, automatically making him one of the club's most important players for the postseason.
9. Garrett Whitlock, RP
Boston's bullpen is perhaps its biggest strength heading into the postseason, and that's because of the Whitlock/Chapman combo at the back end. Whitlock has been an elite set-up man with a 1.75 ERA and 0.877 WHIP across 53 appearances this season.
Starters typically have shorter outings in the playoffs, so we could see the Red Sox turn to Whitlock early and often throughout October if they advance past the Wild Card Series. He's the reliever Boston will count on to mow down the heart of an opposing lineup in a high-leverage situation. That could be the difference between a win and a loss, and that's why Whitlock makes the top 10 over some other very important players.
10. Ceddanne Rafaela, CF
Rafaela rounds out our top 10 most important Red Sox players for the postseason, but don't let his ranking fool you. With elite defense in center field and a bat that made a significant leap this season, he can be considered another X-factor for this club in the playoffs.
If Boston makes a deep run, there's a good chance we'll get at least one signature Rafaela moment. The 26-year-old has a knack for coming up big in the clutch, whether it's with a timely extra-base hit or a mind-blowing catch in center field.
Rafaela's glaring absence during his time on the injured list with a quad injury has highlighted his importance to this club. If he's back to full strength in time for the playoffs, that'll give the Red Sox a major boost.
Honorable mentions: 3B Caleb Durbin, SS Trevor Story, LF/DH Jarren Duran, RP Erik Miller, RP Tyron Guerrero, P Brayan Bello and P Jake Bennett.
They didn't crack the top 10, but that doesn't mean they won't have huge roles in October.
Durbin completely changes the outlook of the offense when he's hitting. He's also been an elite defensive third baseman all season long.
Story has been one of Boston's best hitters since returning from the injured list. There's no guarantee that'll carry over into the playoffs, but he'll at least have to be adequate defensively as the team's starting shortstop.
Duran had a 2026 to forget, and with Anthony in left field and Mickey Gasper likely at DH, he'll probably spend a fair amount of time on the bench. Still, he's the type of player who can change a game with one swing, and his speed is a huge factor.
Miller and Guerrero will have major roles at the back end of the bullpen. Bello (if he makes the roster) and Bennett will be leaned on as bulk relievers. Miller has struggled lately, Guerrero is returning from injury, Bello is unproven in the playoffs, and we haven't seen Bennett come out of the 'pen.

Baseball season’s marathon is coming down to its final sprint this week, and the Guardians are going to find out if they have enough figurative speed to finish on the podium.
The Guardians did the hard work over the weekend by sweeping the Oakland/Sacramento/not-yet Las Vegas Athletics — though they had to come back on Sept. 18 and 19 — and squeaking out a 1-0 win. But style points don’t matter. Plus-one in the win column is all that counts.
The Detroit Tigers begrudgingly gave Cleveland the slightest bit of help by overcoming a six-run first inning to beat the Chicago White Sox on Sept. 18, 11-8. Unfortunately, their offense didn’t make much noise after that comeback, but it gave the Guardians just enough to climb back atop the AL Central alone.
Now, Cleveland takes its one-game lead in the AL Central and a five-game winning streak to Boston to face the freshly playoff-clinched Red Sox for three games. A series at Boston vs. the Red Sox is almost inarguably the toughest series left for Cleveland, the White Sox, and the rest of the wild card orbit of Texas, Toronto and Houston.
The White Sox will head to Kansas City this week, where the Royals are above .500 at home. Then they come back home to host the Colorado Rockies to end the regular season.
Unfortunately for the Guardians, they don’t have the safety net of any tiebreakers against teams in their orbit. A sweep of the Red Sox would give them the tiebreaker over Boston, but that wouldn’t matter as it would keep them in first place in the division going into the final weekend anyway.
The Red Sox also have their rotation lined up for the wild card Series, likely with the Yankees, since they’re close to having that locked in. Meaning Cleveland gets to face Boston’s best starting arms in Peyton Tolle, ace Sonny Gray, and another lefty in Ranger Suarez. So they all have six days of rest lined up into their starts in three-game wild card series.
Boston is six games back in the loss column of the New York Yankees, so catching them is highly improbable. Will that mean the Red Sox will get some players to rest? Possibly. They might be unlikely to push their starters too hard. But then that’s up to the Guardians’ offense to put them in that position to decide.
By virtue of holding Williams back to pitch last week in the opener vs. the White Sox, he’s not scheduled to pitch again until at least September 25 or 26. Cleveland has Parker Messick going vs. Boston in the opener, which also lines him up for regular rest on the final day of the season on Sept. 27, should Cleveland still need to win that game to get in the postseason.
The division title would be the most advantageous path for Cleveland. It would get a bye to the ALDS and host it at home, though the Guardians just did get their at-home record one game above .500 thanks to a 5-1 home stand to wrap up the regular season at Progressive Field. There is also a scenario in which Texas catches fire this week and clinches the second seed as the AL West champ and relegates Cleveland to a wild-card series no matter what. But for the Guardians, everything right now is about being one game better.
If they manage to win the division, then they can line the rotation up how they want for the ALDS.
If they are still fighting for a wild-card spot heading into the weekend in Kansas City, they would need to decide how they need to use Williams and Messick. If WIlliams starts on September 25, he could go in Game 2 of the wild card series on Sept. 30. If Messick has to pitch for the wild-card spot on Sept. 27, that takes him out of the wild-card round rotation at least on regular rest. At the very least, Cleveland needs the wild card spot wrapped up by Sept. 26, so it can skip Messick on Sept. 27, push him to Sept. 29 and have Messick and Williams lined up for Games 1 and 2.
The Guardians will either finish with another AL Central title, the franchise’s third in a row and the 14th in the history of the division, dating to its first in 1995, the last wild card spot, sending them to the worst division winner, possibly Houston or Texas, and then onto the White Sox IF they get past the wild card round. That means this final road trip could be a four-city, two-week tour to play the most meaningful and stressful baseball all year.
Or: They could miss the playoffs entirely. Thinking about some of those losses earlier in the year at St. Louis and Juan Brito’s error and one of the few Cade Smith blown saves. Or another one of his blown saves during the sweep by the Mets with two outs at home after the trade deadline.
Without having any tiebreakers over teams competing for playoff spots with them, the Guardians have to be one game better than any of them for a playoff spot. Be it the division or the wild card. That means winning one game at a time and just needing to be one run and one game better.

Call it a product of injuries or just a slump, but the Red Sox are staggering into the final week of the regular season offensively.
They have averaged 2.82 runs over the last 11 games, hitting .210 with a .621 OPS.
Wilyer Abreu (7 for 36), Mickey Gasper (4 for 25), Jahmai Jones (2 for 18), Isiah Kiner-Falefa (1 for 20), Adley Rutschman (6 for 30), and Nick Sogard (8 for 40) have all gone cold.
Roman Anthony was 5 for 13 with two doubles and a home run over the weekend against the Rays after hitting .137 in his 12 prior games.
The Sox are eighth in the American League in runs scored (678, 4.35 per game). They were third last season at 4.85.
“Just got to stay with it,” interim manager Chad Tracy said after a 5-1 loss against the Rays on Sunday. “Obviously we’ve got to hit and score runs. But we’re getting our way back to health, and we’ll get there.”
The return of two of the team’s top hitters, Willson Contreras and Ceddanne Rafaela, should help.
Contreras has played only four games this month because of a strained left hamstring and a bruised right hand. He started swinging a bat Sunday and hopes to return this week after missing the Rays series.
“It’s getting better every day,” Contreras said Sunday. “We’ll see.”
Contreras leads the team in home runs (27), RBIs (81), and OPS (.905).
Rafaela should be back in the lineup Tuesday after missing 16 games with a right quadriceps strain. He has hit .282 with a .760 OPS, 16 homers, and 70 RBIs.
Caleb Durbin has reached base in 13 consecutive games, raising his on-base percentage from .324 to .338.
Trevor Story has been another positive, hitting .338 with an .869 OPS and 10 RBIs over 19 games since returning from the injured list.
Tests this week
The postseason doesn’t start until Sept. 29, but the Red Sox will get a taste of what’s to come this week at Fenway Park.
They start a three-game series against the Guardians on Tuesday before the Cubs arrive Friday.
The 81-75 Guardians hold a one-game lead over the White Sox in the American League Central. The 87-69 Cubs are tied with the Padres atop the National League wild-card race.
The Guardians have All-Star lefthander Parker Messick (12-9, 2.57) starting Tuesday with Foster Griffin (15-5, 3.67) on Wednesday. Messick faced the Sox in Cleveland on May 30 and allowed one run over five innings.
The Sox have Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez lined up in the series, which could be how they approach the Wild Card Series next week.
Honor for Arias
Shortstop Franklin Arias was named the Eastern League’s Most Valuable Player and Top Prospect by Minor League Baseball. The 20-year-old from Venezuela hit .318 with a .993 OPS in 75 games for Portland before he was promoted to Triple-A Worcester. Sea Dogs first baseman Brooks Bannon also was named to the Eastern All-Star team. The Pitcher of the Year was righthander Anthony Eyanson, who was 4-0 with a 1.69 ERA in 11 games for Portland before going to the Orioles organization in the trade for Rutschman . . . The Sox finished 46-35 on the road, a five-game improvement on last season . . . Assistant general managers Mike Groopman and Taylor Smith interviewed with the Athletics, who are searching for a head of baseball operations after firing David Forst in August. Longtime assistant GM Billy Owens also is a candidate, along with former Nationals GM Mike Rizzo and former Astros GM James Click, who now works for the Blue Jays.

Fans of the Boston Red Sox are about to become bigger fans of the Philadelphia Phillies and San Diego Padres than they've ever been. And fans of the New York Yankees are about to get a renewed interest in destructive weather systems.
With Boston and New York all but fated to meet next week in a best-of-three Wild Card Series, the Yankees are suddenly invested in a chaotic super storm that might interfere with the Sox's meaningful weekend series with the Chicago Cubs. If the Cubs' playoff positioning is at stake - right now, they're tied atop the Wild Card standings with the Padres and one game ahead of the Phillies - these games will need to be completed, whether or not they have any significance to the Sox. Bostonians probably hope the Cubs slip up before they ever arrive at Fenway while the Pads and Phils surge.
It seems very likely these games will need to be completed, though. It also seems very likely these games will be washed out, leading to either a baseball game (or two!) taking up Boston's lone off day before the start of the postseason, or an emergency roadtrip to Chicago disrupting things in a different way.
Will Red Sox insane weather weekend against Cubs hurt their chances against Yankees in playoffs?
Now, counterpoint, we know how much the Red Sox tend to excel when faced with plane trauma or travel trouble of any kind. Does extreme weather also make them superhuman? I, for one, do not want to find out.
Objectively, though, even if they rest all their starters and even if they have zero members of the playoff rotation penciled into this Cubs series, all lined up for the previous showdown with the Cleveland Guardians ... this has to have an effect, doesn't it? It's in MLB's absolute best interest to avoid any nonsense here. Cram a doubleheader into Friday. Tell John Henry he's about to lose some gate receipts and push this whole series to Chicago. The impact on the Wild Card Series is too great.
And you thought this weekend of baseball was meaningless, didn't you, Yankees fans? Joke's on you.
Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suárez will all be out of commission either way, but any undue duress that removes a clean reset point from the Sox while allowing the Yankees to veg out and get in the right mindset can certainly swing things a bit. And if this series is crucial to the Cubs, MLB won't love Boston trying to rest their starters and back away from the competition either. This is about to be fascinating, strange, and a potentially damaging wrinkle in any playoff preview.

The Boston Red Sox are set for a pivotal playoff matchup, likely with the New York Yankees in the first round of the postseason.
It’s been a whirlwind of a season for Boston fans after their horrible start under manager Alex Cora and subsequent hot streak under interim manager Chad Tracy. Part of this hot streak has been the emergence of an elite rotation led by rookies and veterans alike.
Their rotation is so good, in fact, that it’s a real discussion of who will start Game 1 and Game 2 between Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray and Ranger Suárez. And it’s a good problem to have!
Rob Bradford of WEEI shared that Tolle has a “good shot” at taking the mound in the first game of the series. If he gets the ball in Game 1 or Game 2, he will make franchise history as the youngest pitcher to start the first or second game of a playoff series since Babe Ruth in the 1918 World Series, per former Red Sox director of baseball communications and media relations JP Long.
Should Boston Red Sox Phenom Payton Tolle Start Game 1 or 2?
The Red Sox drafted Tolle in the second round of the 2024 MLB Draft out of Texas Christian University. Teams quickly saw that Tolle had the tools to succeed, as he sprinted through the minors.
He would soon have an elite year in the minors in his first professional season, making it all the way to the majors in 2025. However, it was rough sledding for Tolle as he sported a 6.06 ERA in 16.1 major league innings.
Going into 2o26, he was a top-20 prospect. From the start of the season, he has not disappointed. In 25 starts during 20026 (143 innings), Tolle has a 3.02 ERA with 166 strikeouts and just 38 walks.
He has the second-lowest ERA among qualified starters on the team, just behind Sonny Gray. While you could definitely make an argument that the veteran Gray should start Game 1, Tolle has been a monster against the Yankees this season.
In his season debut on April 23, Tolle went six innings, allowing just three hits, one walk, one run and striking out 11 batters. On June 26, he would face New York again, going seven innings and allowing just one hit and two walks with seven strikeouts.
Gray has the regular-season production, postseason experience and fuel, being a former Yankees castoff. However, Tolle seems to be at his best when playing against New York and other AL East teams.
Either way, Tolle will likely be making history not seen since the Great Bambino in over a century.
What About Game 3 and Moving Forward?
Suárez should be locked in for a top-3 start, if necessary. In 27 starts, Suárez has a 3.27 ERA in 143.1 innings with 135 strikeouts. The two-time All-Star is also a formidable playoff pitcher, with a minuscule 1.48 ERA in 11 postseason games.
After him, it gets a bit murkier. While you don’t need a full five-man rotation in the playoffs, it’s likely necessary to have a fourth dependable starter.
Rookie Jake Bennett was cruising through his first dozen career starts. However, in his last seven starts, he has a 5.40 ERA. He may be unlikely to shoulder such a burden in his first postseason. It also complicates things that 2025 Cy Young runner-up Garrett Crochet has been out since late April and will likely be a bullpen arm if and when he returns in 2026.
And perhaps the most shocking positive development has been the improvement of Brayan Bello. In his first 10 games, Bello was a disaster. In his last 15, he has been borderline elite with a 2.98 ERA. This was highlighted by an eight-inning performance on Saturday. If needed, Bello could likely be a starter or bulk reliever in the playoffs.
Whatever the case may be, the Boston Red Sox could be a dangerous team in October, with their monster pitching staff at the head of it all.

Now, they have six regular-season games left to prepare for what is to come.
One big objective will be to get postseason baseball back to Fenway Park for the first time since 2021. After losing in three games in the 2025 AL Wild Card Series to the Yankees at Yankee Stadium, the ending felt too abrupt.
It has already been an improbable turnaround for the Red Sox, surging from 14 games under .500 on June 25 and getting to the postseason. There is a belief within the clubhouse that more magic can happen.
“I think we can make a run,” said rookie lefty Payton Tolle. “I think we’ve got the guys. I think we can get hot. We’re just going to continue to play the way that we play. That team baseball we’ve been playing. You play to get to the postseason and to give yourself a shot to go to the World Series.”
Without further ado, here are some key talking points heading into the playoffs.
What could the postseason roster look like?
C: Adley Rutschman, Connor Wong
1B: Willson Contreras
2B: Nick Sogard
SS: Trevor Story
3B: Caleb Durbin
UTIL: Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Mickey Gasper
OF: Jarren Duran, Ceddanne Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, Braiden Ward
DH: Roman Anthony, Jahmai Jones
SP: Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez, Payton Tolle
Bullpen: Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Tyron Guerrero, Erik Miller, Greg Weissert, Brayan Bello, Jake Bennett, Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck
The most intriguing decision for the position-player roster surrounds whether to add Ward, who set the Triple-A Worcester record with 61 stolen bases this season, as a pinch-running specialist. Dave Roberts, anyone?
The bullpen situation also bears watching. Considering that Crochet hasn’t pitched since April 25 and Houck’s next appearance will be his first in the Majors since 2025, the club will monitor how both rehabbers are throwing before finalizing the roster. This could influence if the club carries Bennett as a reliever. Jovani Morán is another option from the left side.
When does the postseason begin?
For the Red Sox, the fun starts on Sept. 29, when interim manager Chad Tracy’s club participates in an AL Wild Card Series, with all games in the best-of-three series to be played on the road. The Yankees, unless they improbably take the AL East from the Rays, will be the Red Sox opponent in what will be yet another chapter in the richest rivalry in baseball. The only other scenario that can stave off another rivalry match would be the Red Sox slipping to the No. 6 seed. They lead the current No. 6 seed, the White Sox, by four games.
How have the Red Sox performed against the Yankees this season?
Last year, Boston’s hopes of getting a playoff game at Fenway Park for the first time since ‘21 ended when the team lost Game 3 of the Wild Card Series to … the Yankees in the Bronx. So, yes, this would be a rematch between the rivals. In a form befitting the rivalry, the regular-season series swayed back and forth, with New York ultimately taking seven of the 13 head-to-head encounters.
The Yankees swept the Red Sox at Fenway from April 21-23 in what wound up being Alex Cora’s last home series managing Boston. Fast forward to the Bronx from June 5-7, and the sides split, with the middle game getting postponed due to rain. For the Red Sox, their entire season started to turn around with a four-game sweep at Fenway from June 25-28. And for the Yankees, home field for this potential series was essentially wrapped up when they took three out of four from the Sox at the end of August to clinch the season series.
Will Aaron Judge be active for the Wild Card Series?
Judge’s potential participation in the series will be a huge focal point. The Yankees’ captain, limited to 66 games this season, was recently placed on the injured list again with a right calf strain. Though the Yankees have played more games without Judge than with him, his absence could make a difference for Boston.
What happens in the unlikely scenario the Red Sox slip from the No. 5 seed to the No. 6 spot?
In that case, the Red Sox would play the division champion with the worst record, which at this point would be whoever emerges victorious in a shaky AL West.
Which health situations should be monitored as the regular season winds down?
Where to start? There are many to choose from.
Contreras suffered a badly bruised knuckle between his right ring finger and pinkie when he was hit by a pitch on Sept. 17. He admitted he will be out for “days,” but hopes to be back before the postseason. It was a good sign that Contreras was able to grip a bat and take some swings on Sunday.
All eyes will be on Crochet to see if it’s possible to activate him for the playoffs as a reliever even though he hasn’t pitched since April 25 due to left shoulder inflammation.
Rafaela, the Red Sox's All-Star center fielder, has been out since Sept. 3 with a right quadriceps strain but should return before the regular season ends.
How does the rotation line up for the Red Sox?
If not for the near season-long loss of Crochet to this point, the Game 1 starter wouldn’t be in question. Tracy reordered his rotation for the upcoming series, going with Tolle on Tuesday against the Guardians, followed by Gray on Wednesday and Suarez on Thursday. Could this be the same order the Sox open the playoffs with? Tracy isn’t ready to reveal those plans yet.
How much postseason experience does Boston’s projected roster have?
Contreras and Chapman both won World Series rings while playing for the 2016 Cubs. Chapman added another one with the Rangers in ‘23. Kiner-Falefa was with Toronto last season, meaning he got to play in the epic Dodgers-Blue Jays World Series, losing one of the most dramatic Game 7s ever.
Rutschman played in five postseason games during his time with the Orioles, but none beyond the Division Series. Several players in Boston’s young core got their first taste of postseason experience last year in Abreu, Rafaela and Duran. Durbin went to the NLCS with the Brewers in ‘25. Houck and Whitlock are the only players remaining on the Boston team that came two wins from making the World Series in ‘21. Veteran shortstop Story had a solid Wild Card Series in the Bronx last year.
Suarez (4-1, 1.48 ERA in 11 outings, eight starts) had his share of October moments in Philadelphia, and Gray has a 3.26 ERA in six career playoff starts.

When the Boston Red Sox kick off postseason action, if they turn to red-hot rookie Payton Tolle in either Game 1 or Game 2 on the mound, he will make a bit of absurd team history.
It's a real discussion right now about where to slot in Tolle. Boston's top three starters clearly are him, Sonny Gray and Ranger Suárez. Boston is very likely going to face the New York Yankees in the first round of the playoffs and Tolle has had success against the Red Sox's biggest rival this season. Saturday, Rob Bradford of WEEI shared that Tolle has a "good shot" at being the team's Game 1 starter in a playoff series, which would've been a shocking statement a few months ago. If Tolle does get the ball in Game 1 — or Game 2 — he'll become the youngest pitcher to start the first or second game of a playoff series for Boston since Babe Ruth back in 1918, per former Red Sox director of baseball communications and media relations JP Long.
"At 23 years old, Payton Tolle could become the youngest pitcher to start Game 1 or Game 2 of a Postseason series for the Red Sox since Babe Ruth (1918 World Series Game 1),"
How crazy is that? It's been over 100 years since Ruth took the mound in Game 1 of the 1918 World Series and no one has been able to start a Game 1 or Game 2 for Boston in a playoff series since.
Payton Tolle Has A Shot At History
Tolle is 23 years old and 324 days old. So far this season, the big lefty has a 3.02 ERA and a 166-to-38 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 143 innings pitched for Boston. For as good as Tolle has been, it's easy to forget that he actually didn't make Boston's Opening Day roster out of Spring Training.
The Red Sox promoted the lefty on April 23 and he has been incredible ever since. He should get votes in the American League Rookie of the Year race, despite the fact that it's seemingly a foregone conclusion that Kevin McGonigle is going to win the award.
When it comes to Boston's playoff rotation, you can't go wrong with any of these three guys, at least on paper. Tolle, Gray and Suárez are all pitching very well right now, to the point that any could realistically be the Game 1 starter. Tolle has done the best specifically against the Yankees this season and New York struggles against lefties, that should work in the rookie's favor. Gray has been Boston's ace all season and Suárez has plenty of playoff success and is also a lefty.
On paper, any of these three would be a good choice. When it comes to Tolle, it would be historic.

The Boston Red Sox secured a spot in the postseason on Sunday, but the real work is only beginning.
The Red Sox have a date with the New York Yankees in a best-of-three Wild Card series in a couple of weeks. That will be the first team standing between the Red Sox and a trip to the fall classic. If they win that series, they will play another American League East team, the Tampa Bay Rays.
If they can beat those teams, they will have to play the Cleveland Guardians, Chicago White Sox, Texas Rangers or Houston Astros.
The path to the World series is loaded with taolent, but so are the Red Sox. They are on the side of the bracket that features the three best records in the American League. They know they have their work cut out for them, but they are confident. Breakout pitcher Payton Tolle, who could start Game 1 against the Yankees, thinks the team has everything it needs to go deep into October.
"I think we could make a run," said Tolle, per The Athletic's Jen McCaffrey. "I think we got the guys. I think we can get hot. We're just going to continue to play the way that we play. That team baseball we've been having. I'm really just excited to be in this moment again with these guys."
The Red Sox have enough stars to compete with anyone. Roman Anthony is back and healthy. How he performs in October could dictate how far the Red Sox go. On the pitching side of things, Tolle, Sonny Gray and Ranger Suárez will be asked to carry the load. They could have Garrett Crochet back as a reliever as well.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are in the playoffs for the second straight year. The clinch became official Sunday when the Braves beat the Astros, guaranteeing Boston a spot in the Wild Card Series starting on September 29.
The roster is not yet complete. Several key arms are still working their way back from injuries, and the next six games at Fenway Park will determine how the pitching staff looks when October arrives.
One of the biggest names on that list took a step forward this week.
Tracy Provides Update on Crochet
Garrett Crochet is closing in on a significant milestone in his comeback. Interim manager Chad Tracy said the plan is for Crochet to throw a live bullpen session against hitters early next week, with Tuesday as the hopeful target.
"Maybe early next week, a potential IBP dependent on how he feels over the next couple days," Tracy said. "Maybe early next week we'll be able to face some hitters. But yeah, tentative."
Crochet's ramp-up has been deliberate at every stage, and the Red Sox are not going to rush the left-hander into a situation he is not ready for.
Facing live hitters would represent the most significant test of Crochet's rehab to this point. He threw 30 pitches over two simulated innings earlier this month, and Tracy said at the time that everything went well. A live session against hitters is the next level up.
What Crochet Would Mean for October
Crochet's potential availability changes the shape of Boston's postseason pitching plans.
The rotation is lining up with Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez as the likely starters for the Wild Card Series. Tolle has posted a 2.44 ERA across his last eight starts. Gray has been one of the best starters in the American League this season, carrying a 2.76 ERA.
Adding Crochet would give Tracy another weapon to deploy, albeit from the bullpen.
Tyron Guerrero returned from the injured list Sunday and looked sharp. Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, and Erik Miller round out a late-inning group that has carried the pitching staff down the stretch. Tanner Houck continues to progress through minor league rehab and remains a potential option.
Final Word for the Red Sox
Garrett Crochet is not back yet. The live bullpen is tentative. The timeline is still dependent on how his body responds day to day.
The Red Sox have been patient with this process, and that patience could pay off at exactly the right time.
Tuesday will tell the story. If Crochet gets through a live session clean, Boston's pitching picture for the postseason gets significantly deeper.

The Colorado Rockies are 57–99.
Purple Row After Dark: If the Rockies could steal one player
An absurd rule for absurd times: if the worst team in baseball could steal one player from a playoff club, who should the Rockies take?
One more loss will give them their fourth consecutive 100-loss season, and they are almost certainly going to finish with the worst record in baseball.
These are absurd times for the Rockies, so I have devised an appropriately absurd rule to help them out.
The team with the worst record in baseball gets to steal one player from a playoff team.
There are, naturally, some restrictions. We’re freezing the playoff field as it stood before games on Sunday, September 20. The player has to come from one of those 12 teams, cannot be a pending free agent, and you cannot take the player who leads his team in FanGraphs WAR. The Rockies also inherit the player’s existing contract.
No, one player is not suddenly turning the Rockies into a contender. But could one poached superstar at least keep this thing from becoming five consecutive 100-loss seasons?
Here’s the board:
| Team | Off limits: fWAR leader | Highest available fWAR | Other players worth considering |
| Rays | Junior Caminero (5.2) | Drew Rasmussen (4.7) | Jonathan Aranda (3) |
| Guardians | Parker Messick (4.6) | Steven Kwan (3.4) | Gavin Williams (3.4), Brayan Rocchio (3.3), José Ramírez (2.2) |
| Rangers | Ezequiel Duran (4.6) | Jacob deGrom (4.2) | Josh Jung (2.9), Wyatt Langford (2.8) |
| Yankees | Cam Schlittler (6.1) | Ben Rice (4) | Cody Bellinger (3.9), Aaron Judge (2) |
| Red Sox | Willson Contreras (4.1) | Payton Tolle (4) | Ceddanne Rafaela (3.9), Ranger Suárez (3.7) |
| White Sox | Miguel Vargas (5) | Chase Meidroth (4) | Tristan Peters (3.9), Sean Burke (3.1) |
| Brewers | Jacob Misiorowski (6.3) | Brice Turang (5.4) | Jackson Chourio (4), Jake Bauers (3.6) |
| Dodgers | Shohei Ohtani (6.7) | Yoshinobu Yamamoto (4.7) | Max Muncy (4.3), Andy Pages (3.9) |
| Braves | Chris Sale (5.7) | Michael Harris II (4) | Matt Olson (4), Drake Baldwin (3.1) |
| Cubs | Pete Crow-Armstrong (10.2) | Alex Bregman (5) | Dansby Swanson (3.6) |
| Padres | Fernando Tatis Jr. (5) | Jackson Merrill (4) | Ty France (3.8), Mason Miller (3.7) |
| Phillies | Cristopher Sánchez (5.8) | Jesús Luzardo (5.6) | Zack Wheeler (3.5), Bryce Harper (3.4) |
For me, the choice comes down to Brice Turang, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Aaron Judge.
Turang is probably the sensible choice.
At 5.4 fWAR, he would easily lead the Rockies, giving them a legitimate top-end player while immediately solving second base for the foreseeable future. He’s 26, hitting .266/.367/.441 with an .808 OPS, and brings value on both sides of the ball with elite range, strong baserunning and a 95th-percentile walk rate.
It would be a very easy way to make the roster better.
But the Rockies really need starting pitching.
Enter Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
He’s 14–8 with a 2.51 ERA, 178 strikeouts and a 0.87 WHIP over 179 innings. His Statcast profile is just as impressive: 100th-percentile pitching run value, 99th-percentile fastball run value, 95th-percentile offspeed run value and a 91st-percentile xERA.
Pitchers are risky, and Yamamoto comes with a lot of money attached. But it’s hard to argue with either the profile or the results, and the addition of the Penner family makes absorbing that contract a lot easier to imagine.
Speaking of high-priced items...
Aaron Judge.
Judge being available is basically a loophole created by our own stupid rule. Injuries have limited him to just 285 plate appearances, which is why he sits at only 2 fWAR, but he’s still hitting .241/.360/.511 with 15 home runs.
And the underlying numbers are still very much Judge: a .396 xwOBA, .569 xSLG, 94.0 mph average exit velocity and a 57.5% hard-hit rate.
It is very hard to look at that and say, “No thanks.”
After all, Aaron Judge is the type of hitter that, if he were playing 81 games a year at Coors Field, I might take out a small loan for season tickets.
So who are you stealing?

Garrett Whitlock is looking to make a career pivot and transition into the starting rotation. For the Boston Red Sox, it's a strange proposition. The right-hander is one of the best setup men in the league, and that has tremendous value.
Of course, starting pitchers have even more value, hence the higher salaries, but the transition is a risk. Not only does a hurler need to reserve something in the tank rather than just air it out for an inning, but he also needs to have enough variation in his arsenal to turn over a lineup multiple times.
Some Red Sox beat writers don't believe the transition is the best idea. The biggest concern is whether or not Whitlock's health can hold up under a starter's workload. The 30-year-old's past forays into starting have resulted in injuries, making this a serious concern and not just some folks crying wolf.
However, there are still reasons to give it a try. Not now, of course. But in 2027, Whitlock in the rotation could make a lot of sense for a few distinct reasons.
The Red Sox should roll the dice on Garrett Whitlock as a starter in 2027
Presumably, the reason Whitlock would like to try his hand again in the rotation is monetary. On the free-agent market, mid-rotation starters can get upwards of $15 million per season. Look at guys like Chris Bassit and Merrill Kelly, for example, who are making $18.5 million and $18 million this season, respectively.
However, Boston holds options for 2027 and 2028 on Whitlock. If exercised, the Red Sox will pay him $8.25 million next year and $10.5 million in 2028. If he works out as a starter, that's an incredible value.
The next reason to give this a go is the fact that Whitlock has the repertoire to work in the rotation. While the majority of relievers are one-or-two-pitch pitchers, Whitlock has three quality offerings. His sinker is the cornerstone, which he throws 56% of the time, but he has a slider and changeup, too.
The slider he uses at a 26% rate, and it generates a ton of whiffs, coming in at 46.7%. The change gets broken out at an 18% clip, is a weapon against lefties, and also has a healthy 35.6% whiff rate. You might like to see a fourth pitch, just to have a show-me offering, but that's a solid foundation for a starter.
The next point is about righty-lefty balance. The Red Sox have an extreme imbalance towards southpaws. Theoretically, if everyone is healthy, you have Garrett Crochet, Ranger Suarez, Payton Tolle, and Jake Bennett all throwing from the left side. If Sonny Gray retires, Boston will have to find a righty to avoid skewing entirely left-handed.
Finally, the risk is minimal. As long as he doesn't suffer a catastrophic injury, the Red Sox can always stick Whitlock back in the bullpen and have a dominant high-leverage reliever should he struggle as a starter. In that regard, they're playing with house money. They control his future for the next two years, and he's paid a reasonable rate for a setup man, and what would be a steal for a No. 3 or No. 4 starter. At that point, why not take the plunge?

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — The Red Sox will start Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez in the series against the Guardians that starts Tuesday at Fenway Park.
That would conceivably line them up for the Wild Card Series that starts on Sept. 29 with six days rest each.
“Don’t read into that yet,” interim manager Chad Tracy said Sunday before a 5-1 loss against the Rays. “We can line that up still however we want.”
True. But Tolle has a 2.44 ERA in his last eight starts. He also has faced the Yankees twice this season and allowed one run on four hits over 13 innings with three walks and 18 strikeouts.
Gray allowed three runs on nine hits over 13⅔ innings in two starts against the Yankees. He struck out 12 and walked three.
Guerrero returns
Righthanded reliever Tyron Guerrero returned from a 19-day stint on the injured list with shoulder inflammation. Righthanded reliever Wyatt Olds was optioned to Triple-A Worcester.
Guerrero pitched a perfect eighth inning, striking out two.
“Felt good to be out there,” Guerrero said. “If I get a few more games I’ll be fine [for the postseason].”
Guerrero, 35, was called up in May for his first major league stint since 2019. He emerged as a reliable late-inning option, posting a 3.18 ERA over 39 games.
“He’s obviously a very important piece to this puzzle in our bullpen,” Tracy said.
Olds deserved a better fate. The 27-year-old has a 1.20 ERA and 1.20 WHIP in 13 games since making his major league debut on Aug. 17.
“Very tough. He’s thrown the ball great. He’s got big stuff,” Tracy said. “We had to make a roster decision.”
Contreras doing better
Willson Contreras took some swings in the batting cage to test his bruised right hand and came through fine. He said he hopes to be able to do more on Tuesday. “Step in the right direction,” Tracy said … There was no update on Garrett Crochet, who has yet to face hitters. That could come in the next few days … Tanner Houck had a 3.38 ERA over eight innings in four minor league games. Tracy suggested he would face hitters in a simulated game early this week. “Figuring out the next steps at home — and want to figure that out — but no plans for the next outing,” Tracy said. Could Houck be activated? “It’s possible,” Tracy said. “At this point, it’s going to depend very much on where’s the roster at, what are the needs, and then go from there.”… Rays shortstop Taylor Walls showed his baseball acumen in the first inning. With Roman Anthony on first and one out, he allowed Adley Rutschman’s popup to drop. Walls picked up the ball and flipped to second to get the force on Anthony. That left the Sox with a slower runner on first. It ultimately didn’t matter as Trevor Story struck out … Worcester, as Double-A Portland also did last weekend, had its final game rained out. The WooSox finished 76-67. Kutter Crawford was at Polar Park, and the plan was to have him start what would have been a bullpen game. Crawford has not appeared in a major league game since Sept. 28, 2024. He missed the 2025 season because of an injured right knee. He injured his right wrist in August of that season doing yard work at his home in Florida. Crawford pitched three innings in a rehab game for Worcester on April 11 but had a setback and wasn’t cleared for a game until Sunday. “He got to a point where he wanted to go out there and throw one,” Tracy said.

Boston Red Sox right-hander Kutter Crawford was set to make a rehab start with Triple-A Worcester. But with the game being cancelled due to rain, per the Worcester Telegram-Gazette's Tommy Cassell, the club faces a tough roster decision on the 30-year-old starter.
The cancellation also ends Worcester's season. That means the Red Sox will have to decide if they want to roster Crawford during the final seven games of the regular season, and possibly the postseason.
Crawford is currently on the 60-day injured list after suffering a major setback in his recovery from wrist surgery. After a rehab start in April, he experienced issues in his right elbow and has been shelved since. This appearance would have been his first outing in five months.
Red Sox Face Tough Roster Decision on Kutter Crawford
With nowhere to get a rehab outing, the Red Sox will have to decide the next steps for Kutter Crawford. They certainly had some contingency in place if the game was affected by weather.
The first question the Red Sox have to answer is whether Crawford is an option for the postseason. If not, they will likely just shut him down. Otherwise, they have to clear a 40-man roster spot to activate him from the injured list.
If Boston does roster the 30-year-old, it will likely be in a relief role. The Red Sox will likely go into the Wild Card Series with a three-man rotation of Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez, and Payton Tolle. If they advance further, they could turn to either Jake Bennett or Brayan Bello as their fourth starter.
Given the postseason in general, there could be some need for an innings-eater for the bullpen. But Bello and Bennett are further stretched out than Crawford at this point in the season.
If Crawford is done for the year, it will mark the second straight season the right-hander has not thrown a pitch for the Red Sox. That could make him a non-tender candidate in November. But if they do tender him, he won't see much of a raise from his $2.75 million salary for 2026.
It's quite possible that Crawford has thrown his last pitch for the Red Sox.
Red Sox Right Now
The Red Sox aim to clinch a postseason berth in their series finale against the Tampa Bay Rays. They'll send left-hander Patrick Sandoval to the mound.
Boston needs a win or a loss by the Houston Astros to officially clinch. They've already been eliminated from American League East contention, so they would be locked into a Wild Card spot.
The Red Sox have a five-game lead for the AL's second Wild Card spot. So they should lock in their postseason seeding in the next couple of days. That would allow them to set up their rotation for the Wild Card Series. Their likely first opponent in the postseason will be the New York Yankees.

item.content:encoded:
They haven’t clinched a postseason berth yet, but it looks more likely by the day that the Boston Red Sox have a date with the New York Yankees in the Wild Card round again.
This will be the third matchup between these two arch rivals in the Wild Card round since 2021, with each organization winning once. The Red Sox got the best of Gerrit Cole in 2021 at Fenway Park, while the Yankees won two straight elimination games to knock off Boston in the Bronx last year.
This series promises to be low-scoring. These two teams are top three in baseball in staff earned run average. The Yankees have nearly three-quarters of a run lead on the Red Sox among starters, while the two bullpens are separated by 0.01 earned runs per nine.
A lot will be made of how these two staffs line up in a couple of weeks. The first two games for the Yankees, as deep as their pitching staff is, seem destined to be Cam Schlittler in Game 1 and Max Fried in Game 2. However, the Red Sox have serious questions to answer about how they want to line up.
Preparing for this series to go the distance is difficult. If you sweep, you line yourselves up well for Game 1 of the American League Division Series. However, if you get swept, one of your best pitchers may never see the hill.
The conundrum is as follows: Sonny Gray has been their best arm wire-to-wire. Payton Tolle is by far their hottest arm, seeming to get stronger as the season wears on. Ranger Suárez is riding two great starts in a row and is their high-priced free agent with elite postseason pedigree.
But of the three, there’s no question who should pitch opposite Schlittler in Game 1: Tolle.
Stats updated prior to games on September 19.
Game 1 Is a Tone-Setter
The dialogue surrounding Game 1 is that it’s almost a “scheduled loss.” To be frank, it’s hard to argue against the logic. In four starts against Boston this year, Schlittler has a 0.74 ERA, a .174 batting average against, and a 27.3% strikeout rate across 24.1 innings.
Let us not forget the sheer domination he exhibited in Game 3 against the Red Sox last year, either. Across eight innings, he allowed five hits, no runs, and struck out 12.
But the mindset for Boston can’t be that it has no chance of winning. Sure, they’ve been one of the league’s best road teams this year, but the Yankees have the best pitching staff in baseball this year for a reason. By comparison, sure, it’s easier to win against someone not in the Cy Young race. But Max Fried habitually finds himself in the discussion for a reason.
The Red Sox’s mindset should be that runs will be at a premium, so matching the Yankees ace zero-for-zero is paramount. Of the three options, Tolle presents the best opportunity to do so. While Gray has Tolle beat overall in ERA, the Red Sox rookie southpaw is, by far, the hottest arm on the staff.
Since the All-Star break, Tolle has a 2.90 ERA with a 28.2% strikeout-to-walk rate. That ERA drops to 2.53 over his last nine starts. That 2.90 ERA, however, is nearly a third of a run better than Gray’s, and over half a run better than Suárez’s.
Sheer run prevention is the name of the game in this series. Tolle is their best option.
Tolle’s Attitude Is Perfect for the Moment
Every time Tolle speaks, he endears himself to the baseball world even more. But as goofy as he can be in media sessions, he’s all business on the field. Furthermore, he can appreciate the moment he’s in at any given time.
Look no further than his recent start against the Kansas City Royals. Eight pitches, eight strikes, six whiffs, all fastballs. He had the wherewithal to glance at pitching coach Andrew Bailey, grin, lock back in and pick up the final strike of an immaculate inning.
Sure, it’s one pitch in the first inning against a team out of postseason contention, but talk to anybody who’s played, and they’ll tell you how aware they are of when they’re on the brink of something cool. Tolle said as much after the game.
But that moment should tell the world he’s unafraid of going into the Bronx, facing off against Schlittler, and going band-for-band with the likely AL Cy Young.
Tolle clearly cares about what he does, but it’s that somewhat unserious attitude that makes him perfect for the high stakes of setting the tone in a postseason series.
This moment, honestly, seemed set in stone the moment he made his MLB debut last season against Paul Skenes. While any postseason start is high leverage, he’s always finding himself making big starts against the game’s best. He’s always met the moment, and the Red Sox should let him continue that trend this postseason.
The Yankees Struggle Against Hard Fastballs
The Yankees are a deep, talented team even if not all players are at full strength or potential going into October. One area where they struggle, however, is against hard fastballs.
This season, the Yankees have the highest strikeout rate on fastballs 95 mph or harder, to go with the second-worst expected batting average. Only the Chicago White Sox are worse against such fastballs.
They’re even worse this season on hard fastballs thrown by left-handers. Their 33% strikeout rate is the second-highest behind the 61-93 Athletics, while their .191 expected batting average ranks only higher than the Cleveland Guardians.
Tolle isn’t positioned with an elite-level fastball from a velocity standpoint, but it’s comfortably above average. This season, he’s in the 71st percentile with an average fastball of 95.7 mph. Opponents struggle mightily against it as well, hitting just .190 with a .248 expected wOBA and a 30.4% whiff rate.
Tolle throws his four-seam and sinker a combined 68.4% of the time. While that leaves him susceptible to predictability, he varies that look with a cutter that comes in at 88.6 mph on average. He throws that offering at a 19.4% clip.
His strength is his fastball, along with 98th percentile extension. That plays directly into the weaknesses of the Yankees lineup. With Game 1 very much being a tone-setter, there’s no question who the Red Sox should send out there.
Lining It Up After Tolle
Following Tolle, the Red Sox have their two veterans waiting in the wings. Win Game 1, you’ve got two proven performers to help you win one more game to advance. Lose Game 1, you’ve got two experienced professionals tasked with staving off elimination.
The order after Tolle almost doesn’t matter. Could they vary looks and go to Gray to keep the Yankees off the lefty scent? Maybe, but then you potentially run into the same problem of playing with your food. That said, Suárez is much craftier than Tolle, and prone to the hanging breaking ball.
The Yankees have a 99 wRC+ as a team against right-handed pitching, and a 107 against lefties. Gray also took a no-hitter into the eighth inning against the Yankees back in late June, while Suárez was touched up in his last start against them.
What can be said either way is that having two accomplished veterans to follow the rookie gunslinger is a good position for the Red Sox to be in.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. - There was no celebration, but there was a revelation.
The Red Sox couldn't close the deal in securing a postseason berth, succumbing to a Rays 2-1 walk-off win at Tropicana Field on Saturday. But an interesting development emerged along the way. Brayan Bello is suddenly a potential huge part of the postseason solution.
The almost out-of-nowhere conversation about Bello's importance was given an enormous boost by one of the pitcher's best outings of his career. Not only did Bello hold the Rays to just one run over eight innings, but he also struck out 11 and walked no one.
Why was this even more impressive than simply the end-of-day box score? Because Bello managed all those punchouts, along with 17 whiffs, against a Rays team that has struck out fewer times than any club in baseball. No starting pitcher had managed double-digit strikeouts against Tampa Bay, with Toronto's Dylan Cease coming the closest with nine.
Bello matches his career high with 11 strikeouts! pic.twitter.com/NA2a2pDcAy
— Red Sox (@RedSox) September 19, 2026
The dominance was just what the doctor ordered for Bello and the Red Sox, even if starting a postseason game isn't in the righty's immediate future.
While there has been no announcement, it appears the Red Sox are lining up their wild-card rotation with Payton Tolle to pitch Game 1 against the Yankees, followed by Sonny Gray and then Ranger Suarez if Game 3 is needed in the best-of-three series. But that doesn't mean Bello can't have an impact on outcomes from late September into October.
Bello's fastball routinely sat at 97 mph, almost two mph above his season-average velocity. It was a fastball that got nine whiffs, with the Rays coming away with just four hard-hit balls all day.
"That was exceptional," Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy said. "By far and away, his best outing of the year, as good as I've seen him, so, I don't know what else to say, he was awesome. Really awesome."
Bello's appearance allowed for thoughts on what might be in store for his effectiveness out of the bullpen in high-leverage situations come Sept. 29. It has been well-documented what he can do as a reliever, posting a 1.98 ERA in 15 games out of the bullpen this season. But now we're not just talking about bulk roles or giving the Red Sox some length.
This version of Bello can absolutely be a late-inning, high-leverage weapon.
For instance, while we aren't sure of Aaron Judge's health heading into the postseason, if the Yankees' slugger does play, this might not be a bad reminder to put in your statistical back pocket: Judge is just 2-for-21 with eight strikeouts against Bello.
While some naysayers might point to the less-than-inspiring appearances Bello has turned in at Yankee Stadium as of late, including maybe his worst relief outing of the season at the end of August when he allowed four runs over 4 1/3 innings, or the 2 1/3-inning start in Game 2 of last season's wild card round. But before those two, the pitcher had been absolutely nails in the Bronx, totaling a 1.44 ERA in five starts.
Assuming their health is OK, the Red Sox will have Aroldis Chapman and Garrett Whitlock at the ready to help close out games. But with a week to go in the regular season, there is some uncertainty regarding the late-inning options. Saturday, Bello sure seemed like he was ready to help with that.
“For me, it's just showing the team that I'm ready for these kind of games,” Bello said. “Also, them giving me the opportunity to pitch today was a good step for that. And I thank them for giving me the confidence and the opportunity to start again.”
